question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
After Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls both the Corrupted Conscience and (as a result) the Bane Alley Blackguard.

Here's why: Lay Claim ("Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent") targets and enchants Nico's Corrupted Conscience itself (an Aura is just another permanent, so it's a legal target for Lay Claim's "Enchant permanent"). When Lay Claim resolves, it becomes attached to Corrupted Conscience and, per its own text, Analia now controls the enchanted permanent — Corrupted Conscience. Per rule [303.4e], an Aura's controller is separate from the controller of whatever it's attached to, and changing control of an enchanted object doesn't change control of the Aura enchanting it, and vice versa — so Lay Claim changing control of Corrupted Conscience doesn't by itself move Bane Alley Blackguard, and Corrupted Conscience stays attached to Bane Alley Blackguard without needing to be reattached.

However, Corrupted Conscience's own ability says "You control enchanted creature" (i.e., Bane Alley Blackguard). The "you" in an Aura's textbox refers to whoever currently controls that Aura ([303.4e], [303.4m]). Since Analia now controls Corrupted Conscience, Corrupted Conscience's effect now makes Analia control Bane Alley Blackguard as well. This lines up with the Lay Claim ruling that gaining control of a permanent doesn't automatically hand you control of Auras/Equipment attached to it, or vice versa — control of Bane Alley Blackguard changes here only because Corrupted Conscience's own textual effect is now being applied by its new controller, not because Lay Claim reached through to the creature directly.

End state: Analia controls Corrupted Conscience (via Lay Claim) and Analia controls Bane Alley Blackguard (via Corrupted Conscience, now under Analia's control). Nico ends up controlling neither.

This assumes Lay Claim targeted the Corrupted Conscience Aura itself, as the question states; if it had instead targeted Bane Alley Blackguard, the Lay Claim ruling says gaining control of a creature doesn't transfer control of the Aura attached to it — Nico would keep control of Corrupted Conscience, and there'd be a conflict between Lay Claim's control effect and Corrupted Conscience's control effect resolved by their relative timestamps under rule [701.3c]-style layering, but that's not the scenario asked here.

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, with base power and toughness 4/4 (not its printed 7/4).

Here's why. Iroas, God of Victory's own text says "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Devotion to red and white is the number of red, white, or red-and-white mana symbols among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls [700.5a][700.5]. With devotion to white at only 2 before casting Starfield of Nyx, and Iroas, God of Victory itself only contributing one {R} and one {W} pip, Alan's devotion to red and white is nowhere close to seven even after Starfield of Nyx (whose cost is {4}{W}) enters and adds one more white pip. So, taken alone, Iroas, God of Victory's own ability would keep it from being a creature.

However, once Starfield of Nyx is on the battlefield, Alan controls five enchantments (Iroas, God of Victory, the three other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself), so Starfield of Nyx's second ability turns on: "each other non-Aura enchantment you control is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment Alan controls, so this applies to it.

Both Iroas, God of Victory's "isn't a creature" clause and Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" clause are type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 [613.1d]. Continuous effects in a shared layer are applied to the same object in the order determined by when each effect began to apply (and by dependency, if any) [613.6]. Devotion itself is calculated "before any other effects that modify the characteristics of permanents" [700.5a], so Starfield of Nyx's type-changing effect doesn't feed back into the devotion count — there's no dependency between the two effects. That leaves ordinary application order: Iroas, God of Victory's own restriction has been continuously in effect since Iroas, God of Victory entered the battlefield (earlier), while Starfield of Nyx's ability only starts applying once Starfield of Nyx is on the battlefield (later, since it just resolved). Because Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" effect is the later one touching the creature-type characteristic, it adds the creature type back on top of whatever Iroas, God of Victory's own ability did, per the "in addition to its other types" rule for retaining/adding types [205.1b]. Net result: Iroas, God of Victory is a creature.

Starfield of Nyx's ability also sets Iroas, God of Victory's base power and toughness equal to its mana value in layer 7b. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W} (2 generic, 1 red, 1 white), for a mana value of 4, so Iroas, God of Victory becomes a 4/4, overriding its printed 7/4. Its other abilities (indestructible, granting menace, and preventing damage to attacking creatures) are unaffected, since those aren't conditioned on Iroas, God of Victory being a creature.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Iroas, God of Victory was already on the battlefield before Starfield of Nyx entered (as the question states), giving Starfield of Nyx's effect the later timestamp. If instead Iroas, God of Victory somehow re-entered the battlefield after Starfield of Nyx was already established (e.g., it left and came back), Iroas, God of Victory's own "isn't a creature" restriction would then have the later timestamp and would win, making it NOT a creature despite Starfield of Nyx's ability.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears ends up as a 5/4 with no first strike.

Start: Grizzly Bears is a vanilla 2/2 with no abilities, so Muraganda Petroglyphs' static ability ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") applies to it continuously as long as the condition holds [611.3b]. This is a layer 7c power/toughness‑modifying effect [613.4c], making Grizzly Bears 4/4 before anything else happens.

When Crowd's Favor resolves targeting Grizzly Bears, its effect "Target creature gets +1/+0 and gains first strike until end of turn" is split across layers per rule 613.6: the +1/+0 part is a layer 7c power/toughness effect, and the "gains first strike" part is a layer 6 ability-adding effect. The moment Grizzly Bears gains the first-strike ability, it no longer has "no abilities," so Muraganda Petroglyphs stops applying to it [611.3b] (a permanent that stops meeting the effect's condition loses the effect). At this point Grizzly Bears is a 3/2 (2/2 base +1/+0 from Crowd's Favor) with first strike.

When Amia's Archetype of Courage resolves, its static ability gives "Creatures your opponents control lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." Grizzly Bears is controlled by Nathanael, who is Amia's opponent, so this layer 6 effect applies to it. Layer 6 effects are applied in timestamp order [613.7], and Archetype of Courage's effect has a later timestamp than Crowd's Favor's grant of first strike, so it applies afterward, stripping first strike from Grizzly Bears and preventing it from having or gaining first strike again (Archetype of Courage's printed text explicitly overrides the general layer/timestamp result that would otherwise let an even-later effect re-grant first strike).

Because layer 6 (abilities) resolves before layer 7 (power/toughness) [613.1g], by the time power and toughness are calculated Grizzly Bears once again has no abilities (first strike having been stripped, and Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 being an effect, not an ability). Muraganda Petroglyphs' "no abilities" condition is therefore satisfied again, and its +2/+2 layer‑7c effect resumes applying to Grizzly Bears.

Final layer 7c math: base 2/2, +2/+2 from Muraganda Petroglyphs, +1/+0 (still active) from Crowd's Favor = 5/4. Grizzly Bears has no first strike (removed by Archetype of Courage) and can't regain it while that effect lasts.

This scenario only involves two players (Nathanael and Amia), so I'm answering for the two-player case; nothing in the provided rules suggests a different outcome in multiplayer, since Archetype of Courage's "creatures your opponents control" wording would apply the same way to any opponent's creatures regardless of table size.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
Yes — under a timestamp-order application of the layer 4 type-changing effects, Murmuring Bosk ends up as a land creature (a Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, 1/1 green), still under the effects of both Life and Limb and Blood Moon.

Here's the reasoning, assuming the order given (Life and Limb entered first, then Blood Moon, then Murmuring Bosk):

1. Murmuring Bosk's printed type line is Land — Forest [Murmuring Bosk]. Per its own ruling, "Murmuring Bosk is a Forest, but it isn't a basic land" [Murmuring Bosk ruling #0] — i.e., it has the basic land type Forest but lacks the supertype "basic" [205.4c].

2. Type-changing effects (like both Life and Limb's and Blood Moon's) are layer 4 effects, applied in timestamp order [613.1d]. Life and Limb entered the battlefield before Blood Moon, so it has the earlier timestamp and is applied first in that layer.

3. Life and Limb reads: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" [Life and Limb]. Since Murmuring Bosk has the Forest subtype at the point this effect is applied, it becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also still a land, retaining its other types [Life and Limb ruling #3, 205.3c, 305.6].

4. Blood Moon's effect, "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" [Blood Moon], is applied next (later timestamp). Murmuring Bosk is a nonbasic land [Murmuring Bosk ruling #0], so this effect sets its land subtype to Mountain, replacing Forest. question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
No. Sheltered Thicket is currently just a Mountain, not a Forest, so Life and Limb's "all Forests" clause doesn't apply to it, and it is not a creature.

Here's why. Sheltered Thicket is printed as a Land — Mountain Forest, and since it has no "basic" supertype it counts as a nonbasic land under rule [305.8] ("Any land that doesn't have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type"). Blood Moon's static ability says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," which sets the land's subtype. Under rule [305.7], "If an effect sets a land's subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type." So Blood Moon strips Sheltered Thicket of its Mountain-and-Forest subtypes and replaces them with just Mountain — Sheltered Thicket is no longer a Forest.

Both Blood Moon's type-setting effect and Life and Limb's type-adding effect apply in layer 4 (type-changing effects), per the general layering framework described in rule [613.6]. Because Blood Moon entered the battlefield before Life and Limb, its effect has the earlier timestamp and is applied first in layer 4; Life and Limb's effect is applied afterward and checks the game state as it exists at that point. By the time Life and Limb's "all Forests ... are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types" effect is applied, Sheltered Thicket no longer has the Forest land type (Blood Moon already converted it to a plain Mountain), so Life and Limb has nothing to grab onto — it does not turn Sheltered Thicket into a creature. This matches how Life and Limb's own rulings describe it working: it affects things that currently have the Forest (or Saproling) subtype [Life and Limb ruling #3], and Sheltered Thicket no longer has that subtype once Blood Moon's effect is in place.

Note this assumes the timeline you gave (Blood Moon resolved before Life and Limb, and Sheltered Thicket entered after both) reflects the actual timestamp order of the two static abilities' effects, which it does since "entered the battlefield in that order" fixes when each enchantment's continuous effect began existing. If instead Life and Limb had an earlier timestamp than Blood Moon, the layer-4 application order would flip, but since Blood Moon's setting effect always removes any type it doesn't list, the end result is the same either way: Sheltered Thicket ends up as a Mountain only, not a Forest, so Life and Limb still cannot make it a creature. Sheltered Thicket remains only a land (Mountain), keeping its own printed abilities such as "This land enters tapped" and Cycling {2}.

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
The token is a 1/1 green land creature with the land subtype Mountain (not Forest) and the creature subtype Saproling — effectively a "Mountain Saproling," which can tap for {R} the way any Mountain can.

Here's why, working through the layer system: Life and Limb's ability ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") is a layer‑4 type-changing effect [613.1d]. Because the Saproling token already has the creature subtype Saproling, Life and Limb's effect applies to it, and since it uses "in addition to their other types" [205.1b], the token keeps its existing types (creature, Saproling) and gains the additional ones: it becomes a land as well, with the land subtype Forest, while retaining Saproling.

Blood Moon's ability ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") is also a layer‑4 type-changing effect [613.1d]. It only applies to permanents that are lands, and the Saproling token only became a land because of Life and Limb's effect — so Blood Moon's application to this token depends on Life and Limb's effect having already been applied. Under rule 613.8, when one effect's application depends on another, dependency overrides timestamp order, so Life and Limb's effect (adding the land type/Forest subtype) is locked in first even though Blood Moon entered the battlefield earlier [613.8, 613.7].

Once the token is established as a (nonbasic) land, Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" then applies to it. Blood Moon's wording has no "in addition to" or "still" language, so unlike Life and Limb's effect it replaces the land subtype rather than adding to it [205.1b] — the Forest subtype is replaced by Mountain. Blood Moon only talks about the land side of things, so it doesn't touch the creature card type or the Saproling creature subtype, and it doesn't affect color or power/toughness (those are set/modified in layers 5 and 7, respectively, and Life and Limb's "1/1 green" already applies there) [613.1e, 613.1g, 613.5].

End result: the permanent is a land and a creature, with land subtype Mountain and creature subtype Saproling, still a green 1/1 (and, per Life and Limb's reminder text, it's a creature affected by summoning sickness, though that's moot for a freshly-created token anyway).

Note: this answer doesn't depend on player count — nothing about turn order or multiple opponents changes how layers or dependency work here, so it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Alex controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
The 1/1 green Saproling token ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a nonbasic Mountain land (not a Forest) with the ability "{T}: Add {R}" — Blood Moon overrides the Forest type that Life and Limb tries to give it.

Here's why, working through the layers (all of this happens in layer 4, the type-changing layer, per rule [613.6]):

1. The token itself was created as a 1/1 green Saproling creature with no other characteristics (rule [111.3]) — it has no land type or land card type of its own.

2. Life and Limb's static ability says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Because the token is intrinsically a Saproling, this ability applies to it: it gains the card type land and the land type Forest, in addition to its existing card type (creature) and subtype (Saproling) (Life and Limb ruling #3; rule [305.7]'s "in addition to" clause). At this point the token is a Forest land creature Saproling.

3. Blood Moon's static ability says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." This is a type-setting effect (rule [305.7]) that, per Blood Moon ruling #2, causes the affected land to "lose any other land types and abilities they had" and gain the land type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}." The token, having just become a land in step 2, was never given the supertype basic (Life and Limb only adds a land type, not a supertype — supertypes are independent of type/subtype changes per rule [205.4b]), so it is a nonbasic land. Blood Moon therefore applies to it, stripping off the Forest land type and replacing it with Mountain.

Because Blood Moon's applicability (it only cares about lands) depends on Life and Limb having made the token a land in the first place, there's no ordering conflict: Life and Limb's effect must be — and, per the timestamps given (Life and Limb entered before Blood Moon), naturally is — applied first, and Blood Moon's effect applies afterward to the result.

Blood Moon only touches land types and land abilities, not creature types or card types (rule [305.7] explicitly says setting a land's subtype doesn't add or remove card types such as creature, or supertypes). So the token keeps its creature card type, its Saproling creature subtype, its green color, and its 1/1 power/toughness (all set by Life and Limb), but its land subtype is now Mountain instead of Forest, and its mana ability is "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}."

Note: an actual (basic) Forest under the same two enchantments would NOT be converted to a Mountain, because it keeps its basic supertype (rule [205.4b]) even after gaining the creature type, so Blood Moon's 'nonbasic lands' clause never applies to it — it stays a Forest land creature Saproling. This distinction only matters for lands/creatures that become lands without ever having the basic supertype, like this token.

This result doesn't depend on whether the game has two players or more than two — it's purely a characteristic/layers question, not a turn-order or priority question.

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Both the Sapseep Forest and the Saproling token end up as the same kind of thing: a green 1/1 Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, with the ability "{T}: Add {R}" and no other mana or activated abilities.

Here's why, working through the layer system (rule 613.1d, layer 4 for type changes, layer 5 for color, layer 7b for power/toughness). Life and Limb (timestamp 1, the oldest permanent) reads "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types," and Blood Moon (timestamp 2) reads "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Within layer 4, effects apply in timestamp order unless dependency forces otherwise ([613.7], [613.8]); here neither effect's applicability depends on the other's having already applied (Sapseep Forest is already a land and a Forest before either effect runs, and the Saproling token already has the Saproling creature subtype before either effect runs), so plain timestamp order works: Life and Limb applies first, then Blood Moon.

Sapseep Forest: It's already a Forest, so Life and Limb's effect applies, adding the card type Creature and the subtypes Saproling (creature) and Forest (land, redundant) "in addition to its other types" ([205.1b], [205.3c], [613.6]). Then Blood Moon checks for nonbasic lands — Sapseep Forest still qualifies (it never gained the basic supertype) — and its land-type-setting effect completely replaces the land's subtype with Mountain. Per rule 305.7, setting a land's subtype this way strips the land's old land type(s) and any abilities generated from its rules text or old land types (so Sapseep Forest loses "This land enters tapped," its "{G},{T}: gain 1 life" ability, and its Forest-based "{T}: Add {G}"), and it gains Mountain's "{T}: Add {R}." Crucially, 305.7 says setting a land's subtype doesn't remove card types (such as creature) or supertypes, so the Creature type and Saproling creature subtype added by Life and Limb are untouched — only the land subtype is overwritten. Layer 5 then makes it green, and layer 7b sets its power/toughness to 1/1 (all from Life and Limb; [613.6]). Result: Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, green, 1/1, with only "{T}: Add {R}."

Saproling token: It already has the creature subtype Saproling, so Life and Limb's effect applies, adding the card type Land and the land subtype Forest "in addition to its other types." That newly granted Forest land type does not carry a basic supertype, so the token is a nonbasic land once this applies. Blood Moon (timestamp 2, later in the layer-4 sequence) then sees a nonbasic land and overwrites its land subtype with Mountain in the same way, per rule 305.7 stripping the Forest-type-based "{T}: Add {G}" ability (there was no other rules-text land ability to lose) and granting "{T}: Add {R}." Its creature subtype Saproling is untouched. Layers 5 and 7b (both from Life and Limb) confirm/keep it green and 1/1 (it was already a 1/1 green Saproling token, so no visible change there). Result: also Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, green, 1/1, with only "{T}: Add {R}."

One practical note: because Life and Limb's reminder text says these permanents "are affected by summoning sickness," per the Life and Limb rulings a permanent that hasn't been under Aubriella's control continuously since her most recent turn began can't pay the {T} in "{T}: Add {R}" even though it's a land — this matters most for the newly-entered Saproling token and for the Sapseep Forest if it hasn't yet survived a turn change under her control.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's purely a rules-of-continuous-effects question, not one about priority or turn order among multiple players, so it's the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer table.

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Cinder Glade ends up as a plain nonbasic Mountain with no Forest type and only a single mana ability, while the 1/1 green Saproling Creature token becomes a land creature (a Forest in addition to being a Saproling) that Blood Moon does NOT touch.

Why: Blood Moon's effect ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") and Life and Limb's effect ("All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types") are both type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 [613.6]. When two layer-4 effects both try to affect the same object's types, they're applied in timestamp order (the order the abilities came into existence), and Blood Moon's ability has been around longer than Life and Limb's, since Blood Moon entered the battlefield first.

Cinder Glade: Cinder Glade (Land — Mountain Forest) has no "basic" supertype, so it's a nonbasic land even though its land types happen to be basic land types [205.4c, Nonbasic Land]. Blood Moon's layer-4 effect is applied to it first (earlier timestamp): per [305.7] and [Blood Moon ruling #2], setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and the abilities generated by its rules text (so it loses "Mountain Forest," the "tap: add R or G" ability, and the "enters tapped unless..." ability) and it gains only the land type Mountain and the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}." Because Blood Moon's effect is applied before Life and Limb's within layer 4, by the time Life and Limb checks "all Forests," Cinder Glade is no longer a Forest — it's just a Mountain — so Life and Limb has nothing to grab onto here. Result: Cinder Glade is simply a nonbasic land, type Mountain, with the sole ability "{T}: Add {R}." It is not a creature.

The Saproling token: A token only has the characteristics its creating effect defined [111.3], so before any of this the token is just a 1/1 green Saproling creature — not a land, and thus not something Blood Moon's "nonbasic lands" clause can touch at all. When layer 4 is applied, Blood Moon's (earlier-timestamp) effect is checked against the board first; at that point the Saproling token still isn't a land, so Blood Moon skips it. Then Life and Limb's effect applies: since the token has the creature type Saproling, Life and Limb makes it "a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to its other types" [Life and Limb ruling #1, Life and Limb ruling #3]. It keeps its creature type (Saproling) and card type (creature), and now also gains the card type land and the land subtype Forest, per [205.1b] ("in addition to its other types" preserves everything it already had) and [205.3c] (Saproling stays correlated to creature, Forest stays correlated to land). Because it only becomes a land after Blood Moon's pass through layer 4 has already happened, Blood Moon never gets a chance to turn it into a Mountain. As a Forest, it gains the intrinsic mana ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6]. Result: the token is now a 1/1 green Land Creature — Forest Saproling, with "{T}: Add {G}," and it is unaffected by Blood Moon.

(Timing note: this assumes the customary rule that same-layer effects without dependency are ordered by timestamp of the affecting permanents, which is how [613.6]'s framework is applied here alongside the specific rulings on these two cards. All four permanents' relative entry order given in the question — Blood Moon, then Life and Limb, then Cinder Glade, then the Saproling — is exactly what fixes this timestamp order.)

March of the Machines entered third: "Each noncreature artifact is an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." At this point Ore-Rich Stalactite is still a noncreature artifact, so it becomes an artifact creature (this is the same kind of split effect rule 613.6 describes for "noncreature artifacts become 2/2 artifact creatures": the type-change happens in layer 4, and the power/toughness-setting part of that same effect applies later in layer 7b to that same permanent even though it's no longer a "noncreature artifact" by then). So Ore-Rich Stalactite becomes an artifact creature, and layer 7b later sets its power/toughness to 2/2 (its mana value).

Xenograft (naming Saproling) entered fourth: "Each creature you control is the chosen type in addition to its other types." By the time Xenograft's effect is evaluated, Ore-Rich Stalactite is already a creature (thanks to March of the Machines), so Xenograft adds the Saproling creature type to it. Per rule 205.3c, a Saproling subtype correlates to the creature card type, and per rules 205.2b/300.2 an object with both the artifact and creature card types satisfies effects that apply to either. So Ore-Rich Stalactite's type line becomes "Artifact Creature — Saproling."

Now, does Ore-Rich Stalactite's newly-gained Saproling type retroactively pull it into Life and Limb's effect? No. Rule 613.6 states that once an effect's set of affected objects is established as it starts applying in one layer, that same set of objects is used for that effect in every other layer it touches, even if the underlying game state changes afterward. Life and Limb's type-changing portion was evaluated (in the timestamp/entry-order sequence) before Xenograft granted the Saproling type, so Ore-Rich Stalactite was excluded from Life and Limb's affected set at that point — and it stays excluded for Life and Limb's color-setting (green, layer 5) and power/toughness-setting (1/1, layer 7b) portions as well, since those apply to "the same set of objects." So Life and Limb never makes Ore-Rich Stalactite green, never gives it the land type, and never sets its power/toughness to 1/1.

Note on timing assumption: I'm treating the stated entry order (Ore-Rich Stalactite, then Life and Limb, then March of the Machines, then Xenograft) as also being the order in which these effects are checked/applied within layer 4, which is the standard way continuous effects with the same layer are ordered absent an explicit dependency rule in the provided material. Since rule 613.6 already pins down the affected-object set for Life and Limb regardless of any dependency question, this conclusion holds either way.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?
answer:
Both lands keep their own printed abilities and neither becomes a Mountain: Furycalm Snarl remains a plain nonbasic Land with no land subtypes and the ability "{T}: Add {R} or {W}", and Crosis's Catacombs remains a nonbasic Land — Lair with the ability "{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}" (its enters-the-battlefield sacrifice-unless-you-return-a-land trigger already resolved when it entered, since Ainsley still controls it, meaning a non-Lair land was returned to hand at that time).

Here's why Magus of the Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" doesn't apply here. Both Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs are nonbasic lands: neither has the supertype "basic" printed on it, and per rule [205.4c] any land without that supertype is nonbasic even if it happens to have a basic land type. Normally that would make Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" turn both of them into Mountains, which (per rule [305.6]) would give each of them the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" in addition to whatever else they have. However, Magus of the Moon is itself a Creature — Human Wizard, and Humility's text reads "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Magus of the Moon is a creature, so under a straightforward reading of Humility's text it loses ALL of its abilities, including the static ability that turns nonbasic lands into Mountains. With that ability gone, there is no effect making Furycalm Snarl or Crosis's Catacombs into Mountains, so they keep exactly their own printed land types, subtypes, and mana abilities. Humility itself never touches the lands directly, since its text only affects creatures, and lands aren't creatures here.

Important caveat: this exact scenario is a classic "does an ability-removal effect undo a type-changing effect that the removed ability already generated" puzzle. Determining the truly rules-correct outcome requires the full continuous-effects layer system (the specific order of layers, e.g., type-changing vs. ability-removing) and the dependency rule that resolves effects that reference each other's results. Rule [613.1] only gives the general framework (characteristics are built up through a series of layers) but the actual enumerated layer order and the dependency provisions aren't included in the rules I have available, so I can't confirm from the given rules whether a fixed layer order would let the type-change "lock in" before Humility strips the ability. I'm answering based on the plain text of Humility ("all creatures lose all abilities") applied straightforwardly to Magus of the Moon; if the missing layer/dependency rules would instead process the type-change before the ability removal takes effect, Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs could end up as Mountains after all, keeping their own printed abilities alongside the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" from rule [305.6].

Separately, note that tapped/untapped status (whether Furycalm Snarl entered tapped) is a status, not a characteristic (rule [110.5]), and isn't something the question's facts let me determine since we aren't told whether a Mountain or Plains card was revealed when it entered.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes. With Mistform Skyreaver on top of Aiden's graveyard, Volrath's Shapeshifter has Flying (and Mistform Skyreaver's activated ability), in addition to its own granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability.

Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability reads, "As long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, this creature has the full text of that card..." Per rule [612.6], having the "full text" of another object changes Volrath's Shapeshifter's name, mana cost, color indicator, power, toughness, and rules text to match Mistform Skyreaver's printed text -- meaning Volrath's Shapeshifter becomes (in effect) a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with Flying and "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn," plus it keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" text as stated on its own card and confirmed by [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1] ("this card keeps the granted ability in addition to those from the card being copied").

Yixlid Jailer's static ability, "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," is an ability-removing effect [113.10] that strips Flying and the activated ability directly off Mistform Skyreaver while that card sits in the graveyard. Crucially, rule [612.3] states that effects which add or remove abilities don't change the *text* of the objects they affect -- an ability-removing effect like Yixlid Jailer's doesn't rewrite Mistform Skyreaver's printed text, it only strips the ability off that particular object. Since Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability grants it the *full text* of the top graveyard card (not a copy of its current, ability-stripped state), it still picks up Flying and the mana-type-changing ability from Mistform Skyreaver's text.

Separately, even setting that aside: Yixlid Jailer's effect only applies to "cards in graveyards." Once Volrath's Shapeshifter (a permanent on the battlefield) has acquired that text, it is not itself a card in a graveyard, so Yixlid Jailer's ability-stripping effect has no ongoing effect on Volrath's Shapeshifter's acquired abilities.

This analysis assumes Mistform Skyreaver is currently on top of the graveyard and stays there without another card being placed on top in the interim; if a non-creature card were later put on top, Volrath's Shapeshifter would revert to being just a 0/1 blue creature with only its own "{2}: Discard a card" ability, per [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0].

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Dryad Arbor is a land creature that Nickolas controls, and Overwhelming Splendor's text states "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Since Dryad Arbor is a creature, it loses all of its abilities, including its "{T}: Add {G}" mana ability (Dryad Arbor's printed rules text is what normally grants it that ability, per [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]). With that ability stripped away by Overwhelming Splendor's card text overriding Dryad Arbor's normal rules text, there is no mana ability left for Nickolas to activate, so tapping Dryad Arbor for {G} is impossible - not merely restricted. Note that Overwhelming Splendor's second clause ("Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities") wouldn't even come into play here, since that clause only restricts non-mana abilities and Dryad Arbor's ability, while it existed, was itself a mana ability; the real blocker is that the ability no longer exists at all after Overwhelming Splendor resolves. If instead some other effect later granted Dryad Arbor a new ability after Overwhelming Splendor became attached, that new ability would stick, per [Overwhelming Splendor ruling #5], but that's not the case here.

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Watchwolf ends up as a 0/4 red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny" with the type Treefolk and no abilities (still wearing the Lignify Aura). Swab Goblin ends up as a red‑and‑white creature named "Figure of Destiny" with the type Kithkin, base power/toughness 1/1 (currently 4/4 thanks to the still‑active Pack's Favor pump), and it now has Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities.

Here's why. Mirrorweave says "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn," and it targets Figure of Destiny, so both Watchwolf and Swab Goblin (everything Aspen controls other than Figure of Destiny itself) become copies of it. A copy only acquires the *copiable values* of the thing it's copying — name, mana cost, color (derived from mana cost), types, rules text, and printed power/toughness — not any P/T or type changes produced by that object's own non-"enters the battlefield" abilities [707.2a]. Figure of Destiny's activated abilities ("{R/W}: becomes a Kithkin Spirit 2/2," etc.) are ordinary activated abilities, not "as…enters" abilities, so its current 8/8 flying first‑strike Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar state (from having activated its third ability) is *not* copied — this is exactly the Chimeric Staff situation described in the rules: a Clone copying a Chimeric Staff that had become a 5/5 creature ends up as the plain artifact, not the 5/5, though it still has the Staff's ability [707.2]. So both Watchwolf and Swab Goblin copy Figure of Destiny's printed characteristics: name "Figure of Destiny," mana cost {R/W}, colors red and white, type Creature — Kithkin, base power/toughness 1/1, and the three activated abilities as printed text [707.1] [707.2] [613.2a].

For Watchwolf, Lignify is still attached (Mirrorweave doesn't remove Auras) and its text — "Enchanted creature is a Treefolk with base power and toughness 0/4 and loses all abilities" — is a separate, ongoing (noncopy) effect. Becoming a copy "doesn't change any noncopy effects presently affecting the permanent" [707.4], so Lignify keeps overwriting: the copied Kithkin subtype is replaced by Treefolk, the copied base 1/1 is overwritten to base 0/4, and the three copied activated abilities are stripped away by "loses all abilities" — the same way Lignify's ruling confirms it overwrites characteristic‑defining abilities for power/toughness and creature type [Lignify ruling #5]. Color isn't mentioned by Lignify, so Watchwolf keeps the red/white color it got from Figure of Destiny's {R/W} mana cost.

For Swab Goblin, there's no Aura or other overriding effect, so it simply becomes the copy described above (name Figure of Destiny, Kithkin, base 1/1, red/white, with the three activated abilities). However, Pack's Favor's "+3/+3 until end of turn" is also a noncopy effect that was already affecting Swab Goblin, and per the same rule it isn't removed by the later copy effect [707.4]; it keeps applying on top of the new base 1/1, making Swab Goblin currently a 4/4 until end of turn (though its base power/toughness is 1/1).

This scenario is unambiguous about ordering since the question states Pack's Favor fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, so no alternate-timing caveat is needed here.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao becomes a Goblin Zombie (losing its Beast type), turns black, and does get the +1/+1 bonus, becoming a 4/2.

Here's why: Conspiracy's ability is a subtype-setting effect - "Creatures you control are the chosen type" - and per its ruling, affected creatures "lose all of their other creature types" [Conspiracy ruling #4]. Since Allison named Goblin, Leopard-Spotted Jiao's Beast subtype is replaced and it becomes simply a Goblin. This is a type-changing effect applied in Layer 4 [613.1d].

Once Leopard-Spotted Jiao is a Goblin, Dralnu's Crusade's effects - which read "All Goblins get +1/+1" and "All Goblins are black and are Zombies in addition to their other creature types" - now apply to it, because the game continually and automatically reapplies continuous effects based on current characteristics [613.5]. Dralnu's Crusade's "Zombies in addition to their other creature types" clause is also a Layer 4 type-changing effect, but it only adds Zombie on top of whatever creature type(s) the object currently has [205.1b], so it stacks after Conspiracy has already set the type to Goblin (Conspiracy's Beast-replacing effect and Dralnu's Crusade's Goblin-dependent effect settle into the layer in that order because Dralnu's Crusade's applicability itself depends on the object already being a Goblin). The result: Goblin Zombie.

Dralnu's Crusade's color-setting ("are black," Layer 5) and power/toughness boost ("+1/+1," Layer 7c) then apply on top of that, per the ruling that a Goblin affected by Dralnu's Crusade is black only, not black in addition to other colors [Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0]. So Leopard-Spotted Jiao ends up as a black Goblin Zombie, 4/2 (base 3/1 plus the +1/+1 from Dralnu's Crusade).

Note: this reasoning applies regardless of two-player vs. multiplayer, since nothing about targeting a player or opponents is involved here.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant ends up 4/4. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has printed power/toughness 1/1, and it has 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Skullbriar's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," and since Skullbriar has that ability while it's still on the battlefield (the zone it's moving from), the 3 +1/+1 counters travel with it into exile. Per rule 122.1a, a +1/+1 counter "on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield" still adds to that card's power and toughness, so while sitting in exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a 4/4 creature card (1/1 base plus 3 +1/+1 counters).

Duplicant's second ability reads, "As long as a card exiled with this creature is a creature card, this creature has the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it." Per Duplicant's own rulings, Duplicant's power and toughness are constantly updated to match the exiled card's actual current power and toughness (Duplicant ruling #3), not just its printed values -- the only thing that's carved out is that abilities which merely add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's) don't apply while the card sits in exile (Duplicant ruling #2). Counters aren't an 'ability that adds or subtracts' in that sense; they are markers that directly modify the object's characteristics under rule 122.1a in any zone, so they're part of what Duplicant copies. Since Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's counters remain on it in exile and make it 4/4 there, Duplicant takes on those same power and toughness values: Duplicant becomes a 4/4 (still a Shapeshifter, per its own text) as long as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave stays exiled with the counters on it.

This assumes the 3 +1/+1 counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave before Duplicant's imprint ability exiled it, and that nothing (like Yixlid Jailer-type effects) strips Skullbriar's own counter-retention ability before it leaves the battlefield; if such an effect were in play, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave would lose its counters on the way to exile and Duplicant would instead become a 1/1.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands can now tap for {W} only (it produces neither {B} nor {R} nor colorless anymore). Two type-changing effects are stacked on Badlands here, and the second one supersedes the first. Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies to Badlands because Badlands, despite having the basic land types Swamp and Mountain, is itself a nonbasic land card (Magus of the Moon ruling #1 confirms it doesn't grant the basic supertype, it only changes subtype). Per rule [305.7] and Magus of the Moon ruling #4, this strips Badlands of its old land types (Swamp, Mountain) and any abilities from its rules text, and gives it just the land type Mountain along with the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}." However, Conversion's static ability "All Mountains are Plains" then looks at Badlands and sees a Mountain (the very type Magus of the Moon just gave it), so it applies too: per [305.7] again, setting Badlands's subtype to the basic land type Plains strips away the Mountain type and the {T}: Add {R} ability Magus of the Moon had granted, and gives Badlands the intrinsic Plains ability "{T}: Add {W}" instead. Conversion ruling #0, which describes an essentially identical case (a freshly created Mountain never gets a chance to tap for red before becoming a Plains), confirms that there's no window where Badlands is a red-producing Mountain "in between" -- the two effects combine so that Badlands ends up as a Plains-type land producing {W}. Note Badlands does not gain the basic supertype from either effect (per [305.7] and the Magus of the Moon/Conversion rulings), so it's still a nonbasic land, just one with the Plains subtype and only the white mana ability. This is a two-player-independent, table-size-independent interaction -- nothing about multiplayer changes how these static type-changing effects layer.

answer_gold: Only {R}. Both Magus of the Moon and Conversion only apply in layer 4. The effects are applied in timestamp order, resulting in Conversion applying first to make Badlands a Plains, then Magus of the Moon applies making it a Mountain.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones will have flying again. Fleetfeather Sandals grants "equipped creature has flying and haste," and Tightening Coils gives "enchanted creature ... loses flying." Both are ability-granting/removing effects (not characteristic-defining), so they're compared in the same layer by timestamp, and per rule [113.10c] the more recent one generally prevails. When Adriel activates Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability and re-attaches it to Wandering Ones (even though it's the same creature it was already attached to), rule [613.7e] says an Equipment "receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object," so Fleetfeather Sandals's flying-granting ability now has a timestamp later than Tightening Coils's loses-flying effect. This exactly matches the situation described in [Tightening Coils ruling #0]: 'If an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached to it, the creature will have flying.' Since the re-equip happens after Tightening Coils was already attached, the flying grant is now the newer effect and wins, so Wandering Ones ends up with flying (it still has -6/-0 from Tightening Coils, and still has haste from Fleetfeather Sandals, since Tightening Coils never touched haste). Note: rule [604.4] confirms that moving/re-attaching an Equipment causes its modifying ability to reapply to whatever it's now attached to, which is what triggers the fresh timestamp here. This scenario is inherently two-player-neutral — nothing about it depends on the number of players at the table.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
After Titania's Song resolves, Soldevi Digger becomes a 2/2 Artifact Creature — Equipment with no abilities at all. Here's why:

Starting point: Bludgeon Brawl is already on the battlefield and has been continuously turning Soldevi Digger (a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact) into "an Equipment with equip {2} and 'Equipped creature gets +2/+0'" (X = 2, its mana value). This is a characteristic-setting continuous effect, not a granted ability that could simply be turned off (rule 113.12 draws that distinction for the type-setting part), but the equip ability and the "gets +2/+0" text are abilities Bludgeon Brawl grants to it.

When Titania's Song resolves, its static ability says "Each noncreature artifact loses all abilities and becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." This text-changing/ability-removal effect (rule 612.1) and type/characteristic effect apply in the appropriate layers per rule 613.6: the "loses all abilities" part applies in the abilities layer, the "becomes an artifact creature" part applies in the type-changing layer, and the power/toughness setting applies in the P/T layer.

Because Bludgeon Brawl's effect has already been continuously applying (its effect has an earlier timestamp than the newly-resolved Titania's Song), Soldevi Digger qualifies as a "noncreature artifact" (it's an Equipment, which is still a noncreature artifact) when Titania's Song's effect is generated, so Titania's Song applies to it. In the abilities layer, Titania's Song's later-timestamped "loses all abilities" effect is applied after Bludgeon Brawl's ability-granting effect, so it strips away everything: Soldevi Digger's own printed ability ("{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library") and the equip {2} / "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" abilities Bludgeon Brawl had given it. Net result: no abilities remain.

In the type-changing layer, Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger "an artifact creature." Rule 205.1b specifically says that when an effect turns something into an "artifact creature," the object retains all of its prior card types and subtypes. Soldevi Digger was already an Artifact with the Equipment subtype (from Bludgeon Brawl), so it keeps that Equipment subtype and simply gains the Creature card type on top of it — it becomes an Artifact Creature — Equipment. Titania's Song does not remove subtypes; it only strips abilities and adds the creature type/P-T.

Finally, the power/toughness-setting layer makes Soldevi Digger's power and toughness each equal to its mana value, which is 2, so it's a 2/2.

So the final characteristics: Artifact Creature — Equipment, 2/2, no abilities (no equip ability, no granted +X/+0 ability, and no mana ability of its own).

One timing assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield and had already turned Soldevi Digger into an Equipment before Titania's Song was cast (as the question implies with 'Ari controls Bludgeon Brawl and Soldevi Digger. They cast Titania's Song'), so Bludgeon Brawl's effect has the earlier timestamp. If instead Bludgeon Brawl had entered after Titania's Song, the same end state would actually still occur once both are in play, since Bludgeon Brawl's type-setting text still checks 'noncreature, non-Equipment' using the pre-Titania's-Song baseline — but a full walk-through of that alternate ordering isn't covered by the rules text provided here.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
Wayward Angel becomes, until end of turn: a legendary‑less 4/4 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with no abilities at all (no flying, no vigilance, no trample, and no "sacrifice a creature" trigger). Here's why, working through the layers in order (rule 613.1g):

Layer 4 (types): Turn to Frog's "becomes a ... Frog" is a type-setting effect, so Wayward Angel's creature type changes from Angel Horror to just Frog. Nothing else touches type in this scenario.

Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's own threshold ability ("...is black...") is a color-setting continuous effect with a timestamp from when Wayward Angel entered the battlefield. Turn to Frog's "becomes a blue Frog" is also a color-setting effect, but it resolves later, so it has a later timestamp (rule 613.7). Within layer 5, effects apply in timestamp order, so Turn to Frog's blue overwrites the threshold ability's black. Result: Wayward Angel is blue, not black or white.

Layer 6 (abilities): Wayward Angel's threshold ability (timestamp = when it entered the battlefield) grants trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" as long as the 7-card-graveyard condition holds. Turn to Frog's "loses all abilities" effect has a later timestamp, so it applies afterward within layer 6 and strips everything present at that point — flying, vigilance, trample, and the sacrifice-trigger — leaving Wayward Angel with no abilities.

Layer 7: Sublayer 7b applies effects that set base power/toughness (rule 613.4b; see also the "Base Power, Base Toughness" definitions and rule 208.4a/208.4b). Turn to Frog sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1, overwriting any prior base-setting (there was none here, since Wayward Angel's printed 4/4 is just its starting values, not a characteristic-defining ability). Sublayer 7c applies power/toughness-modifying effects, such as the threshold ability's "+3/+3." Crucially, rule 613.6 states that once an effect starts applying across multiple layers, it keeps applying in each applicable layer "even if the ability generating it is removed during this process." Wayward Angel's threshold ability is a single continuous effect whose components land in layers 5, 6, and 7c; even though its layer-6 component (granting trample/the sac ability) got wiped out by Turn to Frog's later-timestamped ability removal, its layer-7c component (+3/+3) still applies, because the threshold condition (7+ cards in the graveyard) is still true and the effect had already begun applying. So Wayward Angel's power/toughness becomes 1/1 (base, from Turn to Frog) + 3/3 (still-applying threshold bonus) = 4/4.

So, putting it together: Wayward Angel is a 4/4 blue Frog creature with no abilities, until end of turn — assuming Ariah still has 7 or more cards in the graveyard when these effects are checked (if that count ever drops below 7 later in the turn, the +3/+3 stops applying and it becomes a 1/1). This whole analysis is about continuous-effect layering and doesn't involve priority or multiple opponents, so it's the same regardless of how many players are in the game.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Immediately after Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up, it is a face-up 1/1 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with mana cost {4}{W}{W}, no creature subtypes other than Frog, and no abilities at all (no flying, no vigilance, and no Threshold ability) — this lasts until end of turn.

Here's why. While manifested, Wayward Angel was a 2/2 face-down creature card with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost [701.40a], [708.2a]. When Turn to Frog resolved targeting that face-down permanent, its continuous effect applied on top of the face-down state: the permanent loses all abilities (it had none anyway) and becomes a blue Frog with base power/toughness 1/1 [Turn to Frog]. 

When Ariella then turns Wayward Angel face up as the manifest special action [701.40b], the manifest effect defining its face-down characteristics ends and its copiable values revert to Wayward Angel's actual printed characteristics: name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, Creature — Angel Horror, 4/4, with flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability [708.8]. However, per rule 708.8, "any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent" — so Turn to Frog's continuous effect keeps applying afterward, exactly as it would to any other creature affected by it.

Applying continuous effects in layers [613.1]: Wayward Angel's own printed characteristics (including its Threshold ability, since there are 7+ cards in Ariella's graveyard) are applied first, the same way a Theros God's own type-setting ability is applied before an effect that strips abilities removes it [Turn to Frog ruling #4]. Then Turn to Frog's "loses all abilities" effect applies in layer 6 and strips away flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability itself — so the Threshold ability's +3/+3, black color, trample, and sacrifice-triggered ability never get generated, since the ability that would grant them is gone. Turn to Frog's type-setting and color-setting also make it a Frog and blue, overwriting Angel Horror and white [Turn to Frog ruling #1]; it retains any other supertypes/card types it might have, though Wayward Angel has none relevant here. Its base power/toughness is set to 1/1, overwriting the printed 4/4 (and there's no surviving Threshold bonus to modify it further) [Turn to Frog ruling #0]. The mana cost and name are unaffected by Turn to Frog's text, so they revert to Wayward Angel's normal values ({4}{W}{W} and "Wayward Angel") once the manifest effect ends [708.8].

Note: had Wayward Angel kept the Threshold ability, it would be black only, not white and black [Wayward Angel ruling #0] — but that's moot here since Turn to Frog strips the ability entirely. Also, no "enters the battlefield" triggers occur from turning it face up, since it already entered earlier [708.8].

This assumes Turn to Frog resolved (and thus began applying to the face-down permanent) before Ariella exercised the special action to turn it face up, which matches the order given in the question. If instead the reveal/turn-face-up happened before Turn to Frog resolved, the same end state would still result once Turn to Frog resolves and targets the now-face-up Wayward Angel, since Turn to Frog would just apply directly to Wayward Angel's normal characteristics.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret (it does not have the Elemental type you might expect from Vastwood Zendikon).

Here's how the layers work out. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability, "Each land is a Swamp in addition to its other land types," makes every land on the battlefield — including Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself — a Swamp [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0]. Because it's a Swamp, Kormus Bell's ability ("All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands") turns it into a land creature with no creature subtype of its own [Kormus Bell ruling #0]. Vastwood Zendikon, which enchants Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, independently makes it "a 6/4 green Elemental creature" that's "still a land," so on its own it would be a Land Creature — Swamp Elemental [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5; 205.1b (retaining the land type via "still a land")].

Conspiracy's ability, "Creatures you control are the chosen type," is also a type-changing (layer 4) effect, but it only has something to act on once its target is already a creature. Even though Conspiracy entered the battlefield before Kormus Bell, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, and Vastwood Zendikon, all type-changing effects continually reapply in layer 4 [613.1d, 613.6], and Conspiracy's own ruling confirms it "can grant a creature type to animated lands and artifacts that would otherwise have no creature type" [Conspiracy ruling #1] — exactly this situation. Once Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature (via Kormus Bell and/or Vastwood Zendikon), Conspiracy sets its creature type to the chosen type (Ferret), and "affected...creatures lose all of their other creature types" [Conspiracy ruling #4]. So the Elemental type from Vastwood Zendikon is stripped away and replaced by Ferret.

So the final type line is Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Ferret (it keeps the Swamp land subtype from Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability and its Legendary supertype [205.4b], and remains a land per the "still a land" clauses on both Kormus Bell and Vastwood Zendikon [205.1b]).

As a side note (not what was asked, but relevant context): for color and power/toughness, Kormus Bell (black, 1/1) and Vastwood Zendikon (green, 6/4) don't depend on each other, so they're applied in timestamp order and the later effect wins [613.9]. Since Vastwood Zendikon entered after Kormus Bell, Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ends up green and 6/4, not black and 1/1.

Assumption: this analysis assumes the four permanents' effects are all currently active and none has been removed or altered since entering in the stated order (Conspiracy, Kormus Bell, Urborg, then Vastwood Zendikon enchanting Urborg). If any of these left the battlefield or the naming/enchant target changed, the type and characteristics would need to be recalculated.

answer:
Frostboil Snarl ends up with all five basic land types: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

Here's why. Blood Moon's effect ("Nonbasic lands are Mountains") has been active longer than Prismatic Omen's, since Blood Moon was already on the battlefield when Prismatic Omen was cast. Continuous type-setting/type-adding effects in layer 4 apply in the order their sources' effects started, so Blood Moon's effect is applied first: because Frostboil Snarl is nonbasic (it has no basic supertype — [305.8], [205.4c]), Blood Moon sets its subtype to Mountain, which by rule [305.7]/[205.1a] replaces any land types it had (Frostboil Snarl's card itself has none printed) and, per [Blood Moon ruling #2], strips its old tap ability and gives it "{T}: Add {R}" instead.

Then Prismatic Omen's effect applies: "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types." Because this effect adds types rather than replacing them ([305.7], [Prismatic Omen ruling #0]), Frostboil Snarl keeps the Mountain type it just got from Blood Moon and also gains Plains, Island, Swamp, and Forest (Mountain isn't duplicated — it's already there). The land also picks up the mana ability that goes with each new basic type, per [305.7] and [Prismatic Omen ruling #0], so it can tap for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}.

Frostboil Snarl remains a nonbasic land throughout ([305.8], [Blood Moon ruling #1], [Prismatic Omen ruling #1]) — gaining basic land types doesn't make it a basic land, and its name/supertypes are unaffected. question: Adan restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. Adan puts [Blood Moon], [Prismatic Omen] and [Winged Temple of Orazca] onto the battlefield with Karn Liberated. What colors of mana can Winged Temple of Orazca tap for?
answer:
Winged Temple of Orazca ends up able to tap for any one of all five colors — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} — but it loses its own printed mana ability ("{T}: Add one mana of any color") and its pump ability in the process.

Here's why. Karn Liberated's ultimate ("Restart the game... put those cards onto the battlefield under your control") puts Blood Moon, Prismatic Omen, and Winged Temple of Orazca onto the battlefield simultaneously under Adan's control (Karn Liberated). That means Blood Moon's "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and Prismatic Omen's "Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types" are both continuous, layer-4 (type-setting/type-adding) effects that start applying to Winged Temple of Orazca at the same moment.

Rule [305.7] governs both kinds of effect: an effect that *sets* a land's subtype to a basic type (Blood Moon) strips the land of abilities generated from its own rules text, its old land types, and copiable effects — but it explicitly does **not** remove abilities that were granted to the land by other effects. An effect that *adds* basic land types "in addition to" existing types (Prismatic Omen) instead keeps whatever the land already has and simply layers on the new basic-type mana abilities.

Working through this: whichever effect is applied first, Winged Temple of Orazca's own printed abilities (its "add one mana of any color" ability and its flying/pump ability) are generated from *its own* rules text, so Blood Moon's setting effect strips them — per the ruling that nonbasic lands "lose any other land types and abilities they had" [Blood Moon ruling #2]. But the five basic-land-type mana abilities ("{T}: Add {W}/{U}/{B}/{R}/{G}") that come from being Plains/Island/Swamp/Mountain/Forest [305.6] are either (a) granted directly by Prismatic Omen if Prismatic Omen applies after Blood Moon, or (b) protected as "abilities granted by another effect" under [305.7] if Blood Moon applies after Prismatic Omen already added those types. Either way, Winged Temple of Orazca keeps intrinsic mana abilities for all five basic land types, consistent with Prismatic Omen's own ruling that affected lands "will also have the mana ability of each basic land type" [Prismatic Omen ruling #0].

So regardless of which of the two simultaneous effects is treated as applying "first" in layer 4, the net result for mana production is the same: Winged Temple of Orazca can be tapped for {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} (one color per activation, player's choice among five separate basic-type mana abilities), but it can no longer produce mana via its own "any color" ability, and it no longer has its flying/pump activated ability, since those were stripped as rules-text abilities by Blood Moon.

This is a case where card text (Blood Moon's type-setting and Prismatic Omen's type-adding effects) directly drives the outcome via the general rule in [305.7], rather than either card's text being overridden.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a Land Creature with the subtypes Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island (and, incidentally, becomes a 1/1 green creature as well, though the question only asks about types/subtypes).

Here's why, working through the three type-changing effects (all of which apply in layer 4, per [613.1d] and [205.1b]):

1. Arcane Adaptation makes "creatures you control" the chosen type (Saproling) "in addition to their other types" [Arcane Adaptation ruling #1]. Realmwright is a creature Apollo controls, so it becomes a Vedalken Wizard Saproling. This effect doesn't depend on anything else, so it applies first.

2. Life and Limb affects "all Forests and all Saprolings," turning each into "a 1/1 green Saproling creature and Forest land in addition to their other types" [Life and Limb ruling #3]. Because Realmwright is now a Saproling (thanks to Arcane Adaptation), Life and Limb's effect now applies to Realmwright too — it gains the land card type and the Forest land subtype (and becomes 1/1 green, though it was already a creature and already a Saproling, so those parts are redundant). Since Life and Limb's applicability to Realmwright depends on Arcane Adaptation having already applied, the dependency system [613.8] puts this second, overriding any timestamp order.

3. Realmwright's own ability says "Lands you control are [Island] in addition to their other types." Realmwright itself was not a land until step 2 made it one. Now that Realmwright is a land Apollo controls, Realmwright's own static ability applies to itself, adding the Island land subtype. This step depends on step 2 having already turned Realmwright into a land, so per the dependency system [613.8] it applies last.

Each subtype correlates to its proper card type per [205.3c] and [205.1b]: Vedalken, Wizard, and Saproling are creature types (correlated to the creature card type), while Forest and Island are basic land types (correlated to the land card type). None of these effects replace existing types — each says "in addition to its other types" — so Realmwright keeps everything and just keeps accumulating types and subtypes.

Final result: Realmwright is a Land Creature — Vedalken Wizard Saproling Forest Island, and (per Life and Limb) also a 1/1 green creature.

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token created by Helm of the Host will be legendary, because Leyline of Singularity's blanket effect ("All nonland permanents are legendary") applies to it independently of Helm of the Host's own copying exception.

Here's why: Helm of the Host's triggered ability creates "a token that's a copy of equipped creature, except the token isn't legendary." This "except" clause is part of the *copying process* itself (like the Moritte of the Frost example in [707.9f]) — it only stops the token from inheriting the legendary supertype *from the copy effect*. Per [Helm of the Host ruling #3], that exception is copiable, meaning the token's own copiable values don't include "legendary."

However, Leyline of Singularity isn't part of that copying process at all — it's a separate, ongoing static ability that says "All nonland permanents are legendary" [205.4d]. Per [205.4b] and [Leyline of Singularity ruling #0], adding the legendary supertype this way doesn't overwrite or interact with a permanent's other supertypes (or lack thereof); it simply adds "legendary" on top of whatever the permanent already is. Since the Helm token is a nonland permanent once it's on the battlefield, Leyline of Singularity's effect applies to it just like it applies to every other nonland permanent Ainsley or anyone else controls — Awoken Demon included. Helm of the Host's exception prevented the token from copying legendary status *from Awoken Demon*, but it doesn't (and can't) make the token immune to a separate rule that grants legendary to all nonland permanents.

So the token ends up legendary. Because Awoken Demon itself is also made legendary by Leyline of Singularity, and the token is a copy of Awoken Demon (so it shares the name "Awoken Demon"), Ainsley will now control two legendary permanents named "Awoken Demon." This triggers the legend rule [704.5j]: Ainsley must immediately choose one of them to keep, and the other is put into her graveyard — exactly the scenario described in [Leyline of Singularity ruling #2].

(If instead the Helm of the Host token were the *only* legendary/nonlegendary pairing in play, per [Helm of the Host ruling #3] normally the legend rule wouldn't apply because only one of the two same-named permanents would be legendary — but that's not the case here, since Leyline of Singularity makes both legendary.)

question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
answer:
After Blood Moon resolves: Snow-Covered Island and Mountain (both basic lands) are untouched by Blood Moon and instead only reflect Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect, while Study Hall and Dryad Arbor (both nonbasic lands) get overwritten by Blood Moon down to plain Mountains.

- Snow-Covered Island: Blood Moon only affects "nonbasic lands," and Snow-Covered Island is a basic land (it has the supertype "basic" per [205.4c]), so Blood Moon does nothing to it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's static ability ("Lands you control are every basic land type in addition to their other types") still applies, so Snow-Covered Island is now a Basic Snow Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest, keeping its "basic" and "snow" supertypes ([205.4b]) and gaining the intrinsic mana ability of each basic type per [305.6]: {T}: Add {W}, {T}: Add {U}, {T}: Add {B}, {T}: Add {R}, and {T}: Add {G} [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0].

- Mountain (the basic land card): Same reasoning — it's a basic land, so Blood Moon ignores it. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove adds all five basic land types to it "in addition to" its existing type, so it becomes Basic Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest with all five basic mana abilities ({T}: Add {W}/{U}/{B}/{R}/{G}), still a basic land named "Mountain."

- Study Hall: Study Hall has no basic-land supertype, so it counts as "nonbasic" for Blood Moon even after Dryad of the Ilysian Grove would otherwise add basic land types to it. Per [Blood Moon ruling #2], "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" This matches rule [305.7]: setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types and any abilities generated by its rules text, and grants only the new type's mana ability. So Study Hall becomes a nonbasic Land — Mountain with only "{T}: Add {R}"; it loses its printed "{T}: Add {C}" ability and its commander-mana/scry ability, and it does not end up with the other four basic types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove would otherwise grant. It is still named Study Hall and is still not a basic land (Blood Moon doesn't add the "basic" supertype, per [Blood Moon ruling #1] and [305.7]).

- Dryad Arbor: Dryad Arbor is also nonbasic, so Blood Moon likewise sets it to Mountain and strips its old land type (Forest) and the mana ability that came with it. However, Dryad Arbor's card type (Land Creature) and creature type (Dryad) are not land subtypes, so they're untouched — per [Dryad Arbor ruling #0] and [Dryad Arbor ruling #2], "If Dryad Arbor is changed into another basic land type, it continues to be a green Dryad creature," and its green color comes from its color indicator, which applies in all zones regardless of type changes ([Dryad Arbor ruling #3]). [205.1b] and [205.4b] confirm that changing subtypes doesn't strip card types or supertypes. So Dryad Arbor becomes a nonbasic Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still green, still 1/1, now with "{T}: Add {R}" instead of "{T}: Add {G}", and it still isn't a spell and still counts as your land play for the turn ([Dryad Arbor ruling #4]). It does not gain the other four basic types from Dryad of the Ilysian Grove, per the same Blood Moon overwrite described above.

Note: none of this changes any land's name, and none of the nonbasic lands become basic lands — Blood Moon only sets the land type, never the "basic" supertype ([Blood Moon ruling #1], [305.7], [205.4c]).
