question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Short version: after all this, Nico's original Thespian's Stage becomes a name-only husk that just taps for one mana of any color, while Alayna's second Thespian's Stage becomes a full, working copy of Temple of Triumph (tapping for {R} or {W}) that keeps Thespian's Stage's own copy-activation ability.

Walking through it:

1) Nico's first Thespian's Stage is already "a copy of Temple of Triumph." Per Thespian's Stage's own text ("…becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability"), its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph plus its own retained activation ability [707.9b, 707.9c]. Its name, per those copied values, is now literally "Temple of Triumph."

2) When Alayna's Alpine Moon resolves naming "Temple of Triumph," its ability reads: "Lands your opponents control with the chosen name lose all land types and abilities, and they gain '{T}: Add one mana of any color.'" Alpine Moon does not touch supertypes or other card types, only land types and abilities [Alpine Moon ruling #1]. This is a dynamic, name-based continuous effect that checks the object's current name, so it doesn't matter that the Thespian's Stage got that name by copying rather than being printed with it. Since Nico's Thespian's Stage is now named "Temple of Triumph" and is controlled by Alayna's opponent (Nico), it is caught by Alpine Moon: it loses all its abilities — the copied "enters tapped," the copied scry-1 trigger, the copied "{T}: Add {R} or {W}," and even its own retained "{2},{T}: become a copy of target land" ability, since Alpine Moon strips *all* abilities with no exception — and it gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" instead. It keeps the name "Temple of Triumph" (Alpine Moon doesn't rename anything) but is now functionally just a plain any-color land.

3) Alayna then activates her second Thespian's Stage (I'm assuming she controls this one, since she's the one activating it — the puzzle doesn't say otherwise, and only a permanent's controller can normally activate its abilities) targeting the actual Temple of Triumph permanent. A copying permanent's copiable values are the target's printed values as modified only by *other copy effects*, not by other continuous effects like Alpine Moon's ability-stripping [707.3; Thespian's Stage ruling #3]. So Alayna's Thespian's Stage copies Temple of Triumph's real printed text: name "Temple of Triumph," enters tapped, an ETB scry-1 trigger, and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" — plus it keeps its own "{2},{T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" per its own wording [707.9b]. Because Thespian's Stage was already on the battlefield, the "enters tapped" and scry-1 triggers do not fire, and it does not untap just because Temple of Triumph is untapped [Thespian's Stage ruling #1, ruling #2]. Now, even though this land is also named "Temple of Triumph," Alpine Moon only affects lands *Alayna's opponents* control — since Alayna controls this Thespian's Stage herself, Alpine Moon does not touch it. So it remains a fully functional copy of Temple of Triumph with its mana ability intact and its own copy-ability intact.

Note on timing/order: I'm assuming Alpine Moon fully resolves (and its naming choice is locked in) before the second Thespian's Stage activation, as the question's sequence states. If instead the second Thespian's Stage activation happened before Alpine Moon resolved, the analysis of what it copies wouldn't change (it still copies Temple of Triumph's printed values), but Alpine Moon's ability-stripping would still apply afterward to whichever of Nico's lands ends up named "Temple of Triumph" at that time.

Multiplayer note: this scenario is framed as two players. If there were more than two players at the table, Alpine Moon's "lands your opponents control" would apply to *every* opponent of Alayna's who controls a land named "Temple of Triumph," not just Nico's — the underlying logic above wouldn't change, just the number of affected permanents.

Also worth flagging: if it turns out Nico (not Alayna) actually controls the second Thespian's Stage, then that Stage's post-copy name ("Temple of Triumph") would make it controlled by Alayna's opponent too, and Alpine Moon would strip its abilities down to just "{T}: Add one mana of any color" exactly like the first Stage.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Because One with the Stars was attached after Kenrith's Transformation, its type-setting effect has the later timestamp and wins in layer 4: Thraben Purebloods ends up as just an enchantment, no longer a creature at all.

Here's why, working through the layers (rule 613.7 says effects in the same layer apply in timestamp order, and rule 613.9 confirms that when two effects don't depend on each other, the later-timestamped one simply wins for whatever it changes):

- Layer 4 (card type): Kenrith's Transformation's text says Thraben Purebloods 'is a green Elk creature...(It loses all other card types and creature types.)' Because its Aura attached first, this applies first, turning Thraben Purebloods into a plain Elk creature (per Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3, it overwrites all prior types/creature types, keeping only supertypes, and there are none here). One with the Stars then attaches later and its text says 'Enchanted permanent is an enchantment and loses all other card types' (One with the Stars ruling #2: it also strips subtypes tied to the lost card types, so the 'Elk' subtype goes too). Since this is a later timestamp acting on the same layer 4 type-setting, it overrides the previous result: Thraben Purebloods is now simply an enchantment, not a creature and not an Elk.
- Layer 5 (color): Kenrith's Transformation's 'is a green...' clause still applies untouched (One with the Stars doesn't touch color), so the permanent remains green.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Kenrith's Transformation's 'loses all abilities' clause still applies, so it has no abilities (One with the Stars doesn't grant any).
- Layer 7b (power/toughness): Kenrith's Transformation's 'base power and toughness 3/3' still technically applies as a characteristic, but since Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature, power and toughness have no functional relevance.

So the end state is: a green enchantment named Thraben Purebloods, with no abilities, still wearing both Auras, but it is not a creature.

One important wrinkle I can't fully confirm from the rules given here: Kenrith's Transformation's own printed text is 'Enchant creature.' Once Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature, Kenrith's Transformation would seemingly be attached to an object it isn't allowed to enchant. Ordinarily that kind of illegal-attachment situation is handled by a state-based action that sends the Aura to its owner's graveyard, but the specific state-based-action rule for an Aura attached to something it can no longer legally enchant was not included in the rules provided to me, so I can't verify from what's given here whether Kenrith's Transformation gets put into the graveyard as a result. If you want that confirmed, the relevant rule would need to be checked separately.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
When Avery chooses to keep the manifested card on top, Trumpeting Gnarr's mutating creature spell goes underneath it, and the resulting merged permanent is face down: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no creature types, and no mana cost, but it also has the triggered ability "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" from Trumpeting Gnarr.

Here's why. As the mutating creature spell (Trumpeting Gnarr cast for its mutate cost) resolves and its target (the manifested creature) is still legal, it doesn't enter the battlefield on its own; instead it merges with the manifested creature to become one merged permanent [702.140c][608.3d]. Avery, as the mutate spell's controller, chooses whether Trumpeting Gnarr goes on top or on the bottom of the manifested creature; in this case Avery puts the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr ends up underneath it [702.140c].

Rule 702.140e says a mutated permanent has *all* abilities of every card/token that represents it, but its *other* characteristics (name, types, mana cost, power/toughness, etc.) come only from the topmost card or token. Since the manifested card is on top, and Soul Summons's manifest ability put it onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature, the topmost component's characteristics are those of a face-down permanent: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond 'creature', no subtypes, and no mana cost (Soul Summons's reminder text: 'Put it onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature'). This also makes the whole merged permanent's status face down, per rule 730.2e, which states that when a merged permanent has both face-up and face-down components, its status is determined by its topmost component — here that's the still-hidden manifested card.

However, the abilities clause of 702.140e is not limited to the topmost card, so the merged permanent also has Trumpeting Gnarr's printed ability 'Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token,' even though Trumpeting Gnarr itself is now the bottom, face-down-irrelevant component. In fact, that ability actually triggers off this very mutate event as the merge happens, producing a separate 3/3 green Beast token, but that token is a distinct permanent, not part of the merged creature's characteristics.

Note: this assumes Avery's manifested card hasn't already been turned face up before the mutate spell resolved; if it had instead already been turned face up into a creature card before mutating, the topmost component's characteristics used in 702.140e would instead be that face-up card's actual printed characteristics rather than the generic 2/2 vanilla face-down stats.

question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
No — after all these events, Mist Dragon does not have flying. Here is the timeline of the continuous effects affecting flying on Mist Dragon, tracked by timestamp order (the method used in [613.7a] and illustrated in [613.9]):

1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves (t1): it puts a flying counter on Mist Dragon (count 0→1). This creates the continuous effect "Mist Dragon has flying" that exists because it has a flying counter; by [613.7a], that effect's timestamp is the timestamp of the effect that created the ability — i.e., t1, when the count first became nonzero. At this point Mist Dragon has flying.

2. April activates Mist Dragon's own '{0}: This creature loses flying' ability. It resolves (t2, later than t1), creating an indefinite continuous effect "Mist Dragon loses flying." Neither the grant-from-counter effect nor this remove effect depends on the other, so per [613.9] they're applied in timestamp order: grant (t1) then remove (t2). The later effect wins, and Mist Dragon loses flying (per [113.10b], an effect that removes an ability removes all instances of it that exist at that point).

3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves (t3): it puts a second flying counter on Mist Dragon (count 1→2). Because Mist Dragon already had at least one flying counter (the count never dropped to zero), this does not create a brand-new instance of the "has flying" ability with a fresh, later timestamp — the ability granted by having a flying counter was already created at t1 and simply continues to exist ([613.7a]: the effect's timestamp is fixed at when it was created, not refreshed by reinforcing the same already-true condition). So the grant effect's timestamp stays at t1, still earlier than the t2 removal effect. Applying grant(t1) then remove(t2) again, Mist Dragon still lacks flying immediately after the second Spontaneous Flight resolves (it does, however, get another +2/+2 until end of turn from that spell).

4. Hex Parasite then removes one flying counter (count 2→1). Mist Dragon still has one flying counter remaining, so the counter-based grant effect is still present, still timestamped t1 (it never dropped to zero, so nothing resets). Nothing about the timestamp ordering changes: t1 (grant) is still applied before t2 (remove), so the removal continues to be the effect that determines the final state. Mist Dragon still does not have flying.

Note also [702.9c]: multiple instances of flying on the same creature are redundant anyway, so the two flying counters were never 'stacking' the ability — having a second counter while the first was already present doesn't add anything extra, consistent with it not generating a new later-timestamped grant.

Assumption/caveat: the key interpretive step is treating the ability granted by 'having a flying counter' as a single ongoing ability whose creation-timestamp is fixed the first time the counter count became nonzero, per the literal wording of [613.7a] ('the timestamp of the effect that created the ability'). If instead every individual counter placement were treated as generating its own fresh timestamped instance of the ability, the second Spontaneous Flight's counter (t3, after the loses-flying activation at t2) would have restored flying, and removing one of the two counters afterward could then go either way depending on which counter's instance survived. Based on the general timestamp rule as given, I'm treating it as not refreshing, so the answer is that Mist Dragon does not have flying.

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan ends up as a -1/1 creature. Fiend Artisan is printed 1/1, and its static ability ("This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard") is a power/toughness-modifying ability that applies in layer 7c [613.4c] — it is not a characteristic-defining ability that sets base power/toughness, as confirmed by [Fiend Artisan ruling #2], which notes the ability only functions while Fiend Artisan is on the battlefield (i.e., it's an ordinary static ability, not a rule-604.3 CDA). Mystic Subdual's enchanted-creature effect gives two separate continuous effects that apply in different layers per [613.6]: "loses all abilities" applies in the abilities layer (layer 6), and "-2/-0" applies in the power/toughness layer, sublayer 7c [613.4c]. Because ability removal happens in an earlier layer than the power/toughness sublayers, Fiend Artisan's own +1/+1-per-graveyard-creature ability is stripped away before layer 7 is evaluated, so it contributes nothing regardless of how many creature cards (four, in this case) are in Aimee's graveyard. What's left is Fiend Artisan's base 1/1 [302.4c], modified only by Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 in layer 7c: 1-2 power = -1, 1-0 toughness = 1. This mirrors the logic in [Mystic Subdual ruling #1] for */*-style creatures whose defining ability is stripped, though Fiend Artisan's case is simpler since its base printed power/toughness (1/1) never depended on a characteristic-defining ability in the first place — only its bonus did, and that bonus's ability was removed by Mystic Subdual's 'loses all abilities' clause, which as printed card text overrides the general expectation that Fiend Artisan would otherwise be a 5/5 (1/1 base + 4/4 from four graveyard creatures). This is a two-player-neutral interaction; nothing about graveyard counting or Mystic Subdual's text changes in a multiplayer game.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The merged creature ends up as a 1/1 with no abilities — the two +1/+1 counters from Glowstone Recluse's mutate trigger never get put on it. Here's why: When Glowstone Recluse mutates onto Maritime Guard and is placed on top, the resulting permanent's other characteristics (including base power/toughness) are derived from the topmost card, Glowstone Recluse, and it has all abilities of both Glowstone Recluse and Maritime Guard [702.140e]. The merge itself establishes these as the object's starting characteristics — base power/toughness 2/3 from Glowstone Recluse, applied in layer 1a as a copiable/merge-defined value [613.2a] — and this is the starting point before any continuous effects from other permanents are layered on [613.1]. Humility, which Nico controls, is a continuous effect that says 'All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1.' The ability-removal portion applies in layer 6, and it strips every ability off every creature, including the mutated Glowstone Recluse/Maritime Guard permanent — this means the 'Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it' ability granted by Glowstone Recluse is removed by Humility's continuous, ongoing effect. Because Humility has been continuously affecting the battlefield since before this creature came into being, the merged creature never actually has that ability at the moment mutation occurs [702.140d], so the trigger never fires and no +1/+1 counters are ever put on it. Separately, Humility's power/toughness-setting effect applies in layer 7b [613.4b], setting base power and toughness to 1/1, which overwrites the 2/3 base established from the merge in layer 1a (layer 7b is applied after layer 1a, so Humility's 1/1 is the final value). Card text on Humility ('lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1') overrides what the general mutate rules would otherwise grant, per the printed-text-wins principle. Net result: the merged permanent (Glowstone Recluse mutated onto Maritime Guard) is a 1/1 vanilla creature — no Reach, no mutate trigger, no counters — as long as Humility remains on the battlefield. This assumes no other timestamped effects intervene; if some other effect later removes Humility, the mutate ability would return and the base P/T would revert to 2/3 (the mutate trigger itself already having failed to fire is not retroactively fixed).

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument remains a Mountain — its characteristics don't change at all as a result of Lizard, Connors's Curse resolving. Before Lizard, Connors's Curse even entered the battlefield, Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" had already turned Forgotten Monument (a nonbasic land) into a Mountain: per Magus of the Moon ruling #4, it loses its old land type (Cave) and its printed abilities (both "{T}: Add {C}" and "Other Caves you control have '{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any color'"), gains the land type Mountain, and gains the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (rule 305.7). It keeps any supertypes it had (Magus of the Moon ruling #1; it isn't legendary here anyway) and it is not renamed "Mountain" (Magus of the Moon ruling #1).

Now, Lizard, Connors's Curse's Lizard Formula ability triggers when it enters and targets Magus of the Moon (a legal target, since it's a creature), causing Magus of the Moon to lose all its abilities and become a 4/4 green Lizard creature with no other abilities. You might expect this to shut off the "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" effect and let Forgotten Monument revert to being a Cave with its original text. However, Magus of the Moon ruling #0 states directly: "If Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains. This is because effects that change subtypes are applied before considering effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which those effects started." This reflects the general continuous-effects rule that once a layer/sublayer effect has started applying to a set of objects, it keeps applying to those objects even if the ability generating it is later removed (rule 613.6).

So after Lizard, Connors's Curse resolves and its enters-the-battlefield ability also resolves (stripping Magus of the Moon's abilities), Forgotten Monument is unaffected and remains: a nonbasic land with the land type Mountain (having lost the Cave type and its own printed rules text), whose only ability is the intrinsic "{T}: Add {R}" that comes from being a Mountain (rule 305.6). It is colorless (lands have no color absent a special effect) and has mana value 0.

question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying. Rune of Flight is attached to Colossus Hammer, and since Colossus Hammer is an Equipment, Rune of Flight's static ability gives Colossus Hammer the granted ability "Equipped creature has flying." Colossus Hammer itself already has the ability "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying." This is the exact scenario described in rule [613.7a]: the "has flying" ability granted by Rune of Flight has a later timestamp than Colossus Hammer's own "loses flying" ability, because a continuous effect from a static ability takes the timestamp of the effect that created it (Rune of Flight) when that's later than the object's own timestamp (Colossus Hammer). When Colossus Hammer is equipped to Skeletal Snake, both of its abilities get new timestamps under rule [613.7e] (an Equipment gets a new timestamp each time it becomes attached), but their relative order is preserved per [613.7a] — the "loses flying" ability still has the earlier timestamp and the "has flying" ability (from Rune of Flight) still has the later one. Since both abilities operate in the same layer (the ability-granting/removing layer, layer 6), the later-timestamped effect is applied last, so "Equipped creature has flying" is applied after "loses flying," leaving Skeletal Snake with flying. This matches [Colossus Hammer ruling #2], which confirms that if the equipped creature gains flying via an effect that (in timestamp order) applies after Colossus Hammer's own ability, it keeps flying. Note that Rune of Flight's other clause ("As long as enchanted permanent is a creature, it has flying") does not apply here since Colossus Hammer is an Equipment, not a creature, so only the Equipment-targeted flying-granting clause matters. This scenario is two-player-or-multiplayer neutral — nothing about turn order or opponents affects how Equipment/Aura layering works.

answer:
Yes, Ogre Warrior has flying. Colossus Hammer's static ability ('Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying') was attached first, but Phantom Wings ('Enchanted creature has flying') was attached afterward, giving it a later timestamp. Neither effect depends on the other, so under the timestamp system the later effect wins for what actually results (rule 613.9's flying/loses-flying example is exactly this scenario). Since Phantom Wings' attachment timestamp (rule 613.7e: an Aura gets a new timestamp each time it becomes attached) is later than Colossus Hammer's, the 'has flying' effect from Phantom Wings is applied after 'loses flying,' so Ogre Warrior ends up with flying. Note this timing assumption matters: if instead Phantom Wings had been attached to Ogre Warrior first and Colossus Hammer equipped afterward, Colossus Hammer's later timestamp would make 'loses flying' win instead, and Ogre Warrior would not have flying.

question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?
answer:
Yes — Ari's Dormant Volcano is still a Mountain. Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect that applies to all nonbasic lands on the battlefield, including Dormant Volcano. Ichthyomorphosis is enchanting Magus of the Moon itself, and it causes Magus of the Moon to lose all of its own abilities and become a 0/1 blue Fish — but per [Magus of the Moon ruling #0], even if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, the type-changing effect it generated continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains. This is because effects that change subtypes are applied in the layer system (layer 4, per [613.1d] and [613.6]) before the game considers whether the source of that effect still has its ability-granting abilities — the order layers are applied in matters, not the order in which the generating effects came into being or whether the source later loses its abilities. So Dormant Volcano, being nonbasic, loses its own land types/abilities and gains the land type Mountain along with the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" (per [Magus of the Moon ruling #4] and the general rule at [305.7], which states that setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land types/rules-text abilities and grants the appropriate basic land mana ability). Note that Dormant Volcano does not become a basic land and doesn't gain any supertype changes — [Magus of the Moon ruling #1] confirms the effect doesn't affect names or supertypes, so Dormant Volcano is a nonbasic land with the Mountain land type, not a basic Mountain card.

question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a 6/6 black Angel Horror creature with mana cost {4}{W}{W} and NO abilities at all — no flying, no vigilance, no trample, no Threshold ability, and no "sacrifice a creature" upkeep trigger.

Here's why, working through the layer system (rule 613.1):

Wayward Angel was already on the battlefield when Humility resolved, so Wayward Angel's own static Threshold ability has an earlier timestamp than Humility's effect.

**Layer 5 (color):** Wayward Angel's Threshold ability ("As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, this creature ... is black ...") applies. Since Averie has 7+ cards in the graveyard, Wayward Angel is black — and per [Wayward Angel ruling #0], it becomes black only, not white and black. Layer 5 is processed before layer 6, so Humility's later ability-removal (which happens in layer 6) doesn't stop this from applying.

**Layer 6 (adding/removing abilities):** Effects apply in timestamp order [613.1]. First, Wayward Angel's own Threshold ability (earlier timestamp) grants trample and the "sacrifice a creature" triggered ability. Then Humility ("All creatures lose all abilities...") applies with the later timestamp, stripping Wayward Angel of every ability it currently has — flying, vigilance, the just-granted trample and sacrifice trigger, and the Threshold ability itself [Humility card text; 113.2a; 109.3 lists abilities as a characteristic that can be removed].

**Layer 7b (base power/toughness):** Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.

**Layer 7c (power/toughness modifications that don't set):** Two things apply here. First, Muraganda Petroglyphs' "Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2" checks Wayward Angel's current ability count — and since layer 6 already stripped every ability, Wayward Angel now has no abilities, so it qualifies for +2/+2. Second, per the established Humility/Opalescence interaction [Humility ruling #2], even though Wayward Angel's Threshold ability was removed in layer 6, the portion of that same ability assigned to a later layer (its +3/+3, a layer 7c effect) still applies — losing the ability partway through the layer sequence doesn't erase effects it was already set to contribute in a later layer. So Threshold's +3/+3 also applies.

Adding it up: base 1/1 (Humility, layer 7b) + 3/+3 (Threshold, layer 7c) + 2/+2 (Muraganda Petroglyphs, layer 7c) = 6/6.

Net result: Wayward Angel is a black 6/6 Creature — Angel Horror with mana cost {4}{W}{W} and no abilities whatsoever. This analysis assumes a standard two-player or multiplayer game state where these are simply the only relevant continuous effects; nothing here depends on how many players are at the table, since Humility and Muraganda Petroglyphs both affect "creatures" generically regardless of player count.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Urza's Saga gets sacrificed almost immediately after Jinx resolves, before its chapter III ability ever gets a chance to trigger. Here's why: Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn," which is a type-setting effect governed by rule [305.7]. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type causes it to lose its old land type ("Urza's Saga") and "all abilities generated from its rules text" — that includes the reminder text about lore counters and all three chapter abilities (I, II, III) of Urza's Saga, since those are all part of Urza's Saga's printed rules text. Setting the land subtype does not change Urza's Saga's other card types or supertypes, so Urza's Saga is still an enchantment and is still a Saga for purposes of the sacrifice rule. The rulings on Urza's Saga cover this exact situation: [Urza's Saga ruling #1] states that "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed." Jinx produces the same effect as far as chapter abilities are concerned (it strips them all via [305.7]), and Urza's Saga remains a Saga (per [Urza's Saga ruling #4], "Even though Urza's Saga is a land, it is also still a Saga"). So the moment Jinx resolves, Urza's Saga has zero chapter abilities while still being a Saga, and Nico must sacrifice it immediately — it never gets to use chapter III (searching for a {0} or {1} artifact card), because that ability is stripped along with everything else. One nuance: the two abilities Urza's Saga had already gained from its first two chapters — '{T}: Add {C}.' and the '{2},{T}: Create a 0/0 Construct...' ability — were granted by effects that already resolved (the chapter I and II triggers), not by the current rules text itself, so under [305.7]'s exception ("this doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects") and [Urza's Saga ruling #5] ("It keeps those abilities for as long as it's on the battlefield"), those two abilities are technically retained through the type change. But since Urza's Saga is sacrificed essentially immediately afterward, that retention is moot — it leaves the battlefield right away. Separately, Jinx's second effect ("Draw a card at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep") is unaffected by any of this: Alexzander still draws a card at the start of the next turn's upkeep regardless of what happened to Urza's Saga. Note: this scenario doesn't hinge on two-player vs. multiplayer rules — nothing here involves choosing a defending player or turn order among multiple opponents, so the answer is the same regardless of how many players are in the game.

question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus ends up as an 11/11 artifact land creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — with flying and infect, until end of turn, with Colossus Hammer still attached to it.

Here's why, working through the layers with three separate continuous effects, each with its own timestamp:

1. **T1 (first activation of Inkmoth Nexus):** "This land becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn. It's still a land." This is a type-changing effect (layer 4 — Inkmoth Nexus retains its land type per rule [205.1b] since the text says "still a land", and gains artifact and creature card types plus the Phyrexian Blinkmoth subtype), an ability-adding effect (layer 6 — grants flying and infect), and a power/toughness-setting effect (layer 7b — sets it to 1/1).

2. **T2 (equip Colossus Hammer):** Once Inkmoth Nexus is a creature, it's a legal target for Equipment under rule [301.5c] ("An Equipment can be attached to a creature"). Colossus Hammer's text "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying" is a layer 6 effect (removes flying) and a layer 7c effect (+10/+10 to whatever the base P/T currently is).

3. **T3 (second activation of Inkmoth Nexus):** This creates a brand-new instance of the exact same effect as T1 — new layer 4 type-change (redundant, already an artifact creature land), a new layer 6 ability-grant of flying and infect, and a new layer 7b set-to-1/1 effect — each with a later timestamp than Colossus Hammer's effect from T2.

Applying rule [613.6] (each part of a multi-part effect applies in its own layer) together with [613.7] (timestamp order within a layer) and [613.8] (dependency, which doesn't come into play here since none of these effects' existence or magnitude depends on characteristics set by the others):

- **Layer 4:** Inkmoth Nexus is an artifact land creature with subtype Phyrexian Blinkmoth (from T1/T3).
- **Layer 6:** T1 adds flying and infect, T2 (Colossus Hammer) removes flying, then T3 adds flying and infect again. Because T3 has the latest timestamp, flying ends up granted again, so infect and flying both remain active.
- **Layer 7b:** T1 and T3 both set base power/toughness to 1/1 (no conflict, same value).
- **Layer 7c:** Colossus Hammer's +10/+10 is applied on top of that 1/1 base, giving a final 11/11.

Colossus Hammer's printed text ("Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying") is a general rule-overriding card effect, but because Inkmoth Nexus's own ability is reactivated afterward with a later timestamp, the later flying-granting effect simply supersedes the earlier flying-removal effect in layer 6 — this isn't a contradiction of Colossus Hammer's text, just normal timestamp layering.

So the final state: Inkmoth Nexus is a colorless 11/11 artifact land creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth — with flying and infect, still a land, equipped with Colossus Hammer, until end of turn.

(Note: whether it can attack or be tapped for mana this turn separately depends on how long Aaden has controlled it and summoning sickness, per Inkmoth Nexus's rulings, but that doesn't change its characteristics as asked.)

question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?
answer:
Ari ends up with three copies of Aeve, Progenitor Ooze on the battlefield — one nontoken (the original spell) and two tokens (from storm) — and because Nadia controls Humility, all three lose their rules text and have their base power/toughness overwritten to 1/1, though the +1/+1 counters they entered with still stick around, giving them 1/1, 2/2, and 3/3 respectively. None of them are forced into the legend rule.

Step by step:

1. **Storm makes two copies.** Aeve, Progenitor Ooze has Storm, which copies the spell for each spell cast before it this turn; two spells were cast before Aeve, so two copies are put on the stack, and per the storm rules those copies become tokens. A copy of a spell has the same characteristics (including all of Aeve's printed abilities) as the original [707.10e]. These two token copies resolve first (they were stacked on top of the original spell), and the original Aeve spell resolves last, becoming a permanent that is *not* a token [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2].

2. **Entering-the-battlefield counters.** Aeve's own text says "Aeve enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each other Ooze you control." Per the official ruling, the storm copies enter one at a time, followed by the original: the first token enters with 0 counters (no other Oozes yet), the second token enters with 1 counter (one Ooze already on the battlefield), and the original Aeve enters with 2 counters (two Oozes already there) [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2]. This replacement effect governs how each permanent comes into being as part of the entering-the-battlefield event itself [616.1g], so it applies to each Aeve, Progenitor Ooze as normal even though Humility is in play — Humility only starts continuously stripping abilities from a creature once that creature already exists on the battlefield.

3. **Legendary status.** Aeve's text also says "Aeve isn't legendary if it's a token." This is a supertype-removing effect, which is a layer 4 (type-changing) effect generated by that ability. Humility's "all creatures lose all abilities" is a layer 6 effect. Because layer 4 is processed before layer 6, the illustrative Humility ruling shows that a layer-4 effect generated by an ability locks in before that same ability is stripped away in layer 6 — the loss of the ability afterward doesn't retroactively undo the type change it already caused [Humility ruling #2]. Applying that same layer logic here, each of the two Aeve tokens is already non-legendary (via its own "isn't legendary if it's a token" ability) before Humility's layer-6 effect removes that ability going forward. So you never actually have more than one legendary permanent named "Aeve, Progenitor Ooze" at once — only the original, nontoken Aeve is legendary — and the legend rule is not triggered.

4. **Final characteristics.** Once everything has resolved and state-based actions are checked, Humility's static ability [Humility] makes all three creatures lose all their abilities (storm, the enters-with-counters ability, and "isn't legendary if it's a token" all stop functioning going forward) and sets each of their base power/toughness to 1/1. The +1/+1 counters they already received when entering are physical counters, not abilities, so Humility doesn't remove them; they still add on top of the 1/1 base. That gives:
 - Token Aeve #1: 1/1 base + 0 counters = **1/1**, Ooze creature token, no abilities, not legendary.
 - Token Aeve #2: 1/1 base + 1 counter = **2/2**, Ooze creature token, no abilities, not legendary.
 - Original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze: 1/1 base + 2 counters = **3/3**, Legendary Creature — Ooze, no abilities.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Humility was already on the battlefield before Ari cast Aeve, Progenitor Ooze, so its effect is active throughout the whole resolution (storm copies, entering, and counter placement). If Humility instead entered only after all three Aeve permanents were already on the battlefield with their counters, the end result on power/toughness and ability loss would be the same (Humility applies continuously to whatever creatures exist), but the legend-rule timing wouldn't even be in question since by then the tokens would already be locked in as non-legendary the same way.

question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
One with the Stars fails to resolve and goes to Natalie's graveyard; when the crew ability then resolves, Capenna Express simply becomes a 6/6 artifact creature until end of turn, completely unaffected by One with the Stars.

Here's why: Allen's crew activation went on the stack first, so when Natalie casts One with the Stars on top of it, the stack order (top to bottom) is One with the Stars, then the crew ability. One with the Stars resolves first — before the crew ability ever resolves. One with the Stars's enchant restriction is "Enchant creature or enchantment" (per its printed text). At the moment it tries to resolve, Capenna Express is still just an artifact Vehicle — it has not yet become a creature, because Crew is an activated ability whose effect ("This permanent becomes an artifact creature until end of turn") only happens when that ability itself resolves [702.122a], and that ability hasn't resolved yet. Capenna Express is also not an enchantment. So at the time One with the Stars checks its target's legality, Capenna Express is neither a creature nor an enchantment, making it an illegal target [608.2b, 608.3b]. Because all of One with the Stars's targets are illegal, it doesn't resolve — it's removed from the stack and, being an Aura that can't legally attach to its target, put into Natalie's graveyard rather than entering the battlefield [303.4i, 608.2b].

After that, the crew ability resolves on its own terms: since Crew 3's cost was paid, Capenna Express becomes an artifact creature until end of turn [702.122a], with no lingering effect from One with the Stars (it never attached, so it never applied).

Note the timing assumption: I'm assuming Natalie cast One with the Stars while the crew ability was still unresolved and Capenna Express was still just a Vehicle (as the question states). If instead Natalie had waited until after the crew ability resolved (so Capenna Express was already a temporary artifact creature) before casting One with the Stars, the Aura would have a legal target, would resolve normally, and — per the card's ruling — would make Capenna Express permanently an enchantment (losing its creature/artifact types) even after the crew effect's "until end of turn" duration expired [One with the Stars ruling #1]. That is not what happened here, since the casting/targeting occurred before the crew ability resolved.

This analysis holds the same whether the game has two players or more than two, since it concerns only stack resolution order and targeting legality, not player-order or defending-player rules.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Aitana casts [Finale of Devastation] with X = 10. Will the creature they find have haste?
answer:
Yes — the creature that Aitana finds with Finale of Devastation will have haste, even though Nico controls Humility.

Humility is a static ability that creates a continuous effect saying "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" [Humility]. This is an ability-removing effect under rule [113.10b] and [113.10], and it applies in layer 6 (the ability layer) with a timestamp from whenever Humility entered the battlefield — which is before Aitana's Finale of Devastation resolves.

When X is 10 or more, Finale of Devastation's resolution creates a new continuous effect (until end of turn) that gives creatures you control +X/+X and haste [Finale of Devastation ruling #2]. Since this effect is created when Finale of Devastation resolves — after Humility is already on the battlefield — it has a later timestamp than Humility's ability-removal effect. Rule [113.10c] states that when two or more effects add and remove the same ability, the most recent one prevails. Because Finale of Devastation's haste-granting effect is the more recent of the two, it wins, and the found creature keeps haste despite Humility trying to strip all abilities.

The creature will still have base power/toughness set to 1/1 by Humility in layer 7b before Finale of Devastation's +10/+10 is applied in a later layer step, so it ends up as an 11/11 (unmodified base 1/1, plus +10/+10) with haste — but that power/toughness math isn't what you asked about; the key point is it does have haste.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Humility was already on the battlefield with an established timestamp before Aitana cast Finale of Devastation, which is what the question describes (Nico already controls Humility). If instead Humility somehow entered the battlefield *after* Finale of Devastation's continuous effect was already created, Humility's more recent ability-removal would instead strip the haste — but that's not the scenario given.

question: Avery's [Unlicensed Hearse] has exiled five cards, and they activate its crew ability. After that resolves, Avery casts [Dress Down]. What does Unlicensed Hearse look like?
answer:
Unlicensed Hearse becomes a 0/0 artifact creature and is immediately put into Avery's graveyard as a state-based action.

Here's why: When Avery activates the crew ability, Unlicensed Hearse becomes an artifact creature (with power/toughness equal to the number of cards exiled with it — currently 5, so it's a 5/5). Then Dress Down resolves, entering the battlefield and drawing Avery a card. Dress Down's static ability says "Creatures lose all abilities," and Unlicensed Hearse is currently a creature, so it loses all of its printed abilities — both its activated ability ("{T}: Exile up to two target cards from a single graveyard") and, critically, the characteristic-defining ability that reads "Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards exiled with it."

Once that power/toughness-setting ability is gone, nothing is defining Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness anymore. Unlicensed Hearse's own ruling confirms how this situation is handled: [Unlicensed Hearse ruling #0] states that if the ability hasn't produced a value (e.g., because it was activated before any cards were exiled), Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are 0/0, and "unless there is another effect increasing its toughness, it will be put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action." The same result applies here — with the defining ability removed by Dress Down, Unlicensed Hearse has no power/toughness value being set, so it is treated as 0/0. Since it is still a creature (crewed) with 0 toughness, it dies to a state-based action and goes to Avery's graveyard as soon as Dress Down finishes resolving (before anyone gets priority to respond, since state-based actions are checked before priority is passed).

Note: the five cards previously exiled by Unlicensed Hearse's first ability remain in exile — losing the linked ability that referenced "cards exiled with it" [406.6][607.2a] doesn't return them anywhere; it just stops that ability from being able to reference them, which no longer matters once Unlicensed Hearse is gone. Also, [Dress Down ruling #0] confirms Dress Down only strips abilities the permanent already has; it doesn't stop it from being animated as a creature by crew in the first place, which is why Unlicensed Hearse is a creature (and thus affected) when Dress Down's effect applies.

This assumes Dress Down is cast and resolves after the crew activation has already resolved and Unlicensed Hearse is already an animated creature, exactly as the question states; if Dress Down had somehow resolved before crewing, Unlicensed Hearse wouldn't be a creature yet and "Creatures lose all abilities" wouldn't apply to it at that moment (though it would still lose the ability the instant it later became a creature, per the same static effect, leading to the same 0/0 death).

question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — once Opalescence resolves, Karametra, God of Harvests becomes a 5/5 creature, and this holds true despite Alex's devotion to green and white being only 2 (not 7 or more).

Here's why: Opalescence's ability says "Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types and has base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Karametra, God of Harvests is an enchantment even when its own devotion-based ability strips its creature type — [Karametra, God of Harvests ruling #15] confirms that when Karametra stops being a creature, it still remains a legendary enchantment. So Karametra, God of Harvests qualifies as an "other non-Aura enchantment" for Opalescence's purposes.

Both Karametra's devotion-based type-changing ability and Opalescence's type-changing ability operate in layer 4, and layer 4 effects (outside layer 1's sublayers) are applied in timestamp order [613.2, 613.2a]. Since Alex already controlled Karametra, God of Harvests before casting Opalescence, Karametra's static ability has the earlier timestamp and Opalescence's has the later one. Applying them in order: Karametra's own ability first tries to make it not a creature (since devotion to green/white is only 2, well under 7), but then Opalescence's later-timestamped effect makes it a creature again. This is exactly analogous to the documented Humility/Opalescence interaction: when the "turns into a creature" enchantment (Opalescence) has a later timestamp than the other permanent's own type-setting ability, Opalescence's type change is the one that ends up applying [Opalescence ruling #1] [Opalescence ruling #3]. So here, because Opalescence's timestamp is later, Karametra, God of Harvests ends up being a creature — Alex's low devotion doesn't save it from Opalescence.

For power and toughness, Opalescence sets Karametra, God of Harvests's base power and toughness equal to its mana value. Karametra, God of Harvests has mana cost {3}{G}{W}, which is a mana value of 5. Since there's no other characteristic-defining or setting effect competing for power/toughness here (Karametra's own P/T of 6/7 is just its printed value, not a characteristic-defining ability under rule 604.3/208.2a), Opalescence's layer 7b effect simply sets it: Karametra, God of Harvests becomes a 5/5.

Note: Karametra, God of Harvests's other abilities (Indestructible, the search trigger) still function regardless of whether it's a creature, per [Karametra, God of Harvests ruling #22], so those are unaffected either way.

This assumes the timing you described — Karametra, God of Harvests was already on the battlefield when Opalescence was cast and resolved, giving Opalescence the later timestamp. If instead Opalescence had somehow been on the battlefield first and Karametra, God of Harvests entered afterward, the timestamp order would flip and Karametra's own devotion-based ability would have the later timestamp, meaning it would turn itself back into a non-creature after Opalescence's effect applied — in that scenario, with devotion only 2, Karametra, God of Harvests would NOT be a creature.

question: Autumn animates [Inkmoth Nexus] and attacks with it. Nayeli then flashes in [Dress Down]. What does Inkmoth Nexus look like?
answer:
After Dress Down resolves, Inkmoth Nexus is still a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature that is attacking, but it has no abilities at all — no flying, no infect, and not even its own printed mana ability or its "{1}: become a creature" ability.

Here's why. Inkmoth Nexus's own ability reads "This land becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn. It's still a land." That single sentence actually does several things in different layers: it sets Inkmoth Nexus's types (artifact creature, still a land, with the creature type Phyrexian Blinkmoth) in layer 4, it sets its power/toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b, and it grants it the abilities flying and infect in layer 6 [613.6][613.4b]. Type-changing and power/toughness-setting are not "abilities" — they're characteristic-setting effects, distinct from granted abilities [113.12][205.1b].

When Nayeli flashes in Dress Down, its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" is a layer-6 effect. Because it starts affecting Inkmoth Nexus later than Inkmoth Nexus's own animate ability did (Dress Down's effect has the later timestamp), it applies on top and strips away every ability Inkmoth Nexus currently has [613.7][613.4b]. That includes the flying and infect that were granted by its own ability, and it also includes Inkmoth Nexus's two printed abilities ("{T}: Add {C}" and "{1}: This land becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn") — because Inkmoth Nexus is currently a creature, "creatures lose all abilities" strips its native abilities too, not just abilities granted by other effects (Dress Down card text, Inkmoth Nexus card text).

What Dress Down does NOT undo is the type-change (layer 4) and the 1/1 power/toughness (layer 7b), since those were never abilities to begin with — they're characteristic-setting effects that keep applying to the same object even though the ability that generated them is now itself gone/irrelevant to layer 6 [613.6][113.12]. So Inkmoth Nexus remains a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature, still attacking (losing abilities doesn't remove a creature from combat), but with a completely blank ability box — no flying, no infect, no mana ability, nothing.

This is a two-player-consistent analysis; nothing here depends on the number of players at the table.

question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?
answer:
The two 1/1 colorless Spirit creature tokens from Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's Channel ability still get created and still have haste, because the ability that grants them haste takes effect *after* Dress Down is already on the battlefield.

Here's the sequence: Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's Channel ability ("Create two 1/1 colorless Spirit creature tokens. They gain haste until end of turn.") is activated and put on the stack. Nehemiah then casts Dress Down in response, so it goes on top of the stack and resolves first. Dress Down enters the battlefield (drawing Nehemiah a card) and its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" begins applying continuously to creatures on the battlefield [Dress Down text].

After Dress Down has resolved, Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's Channel ability resolves, and the two 1/1 colorless Spirit tokens are created [111.1] [Create]. As part of that same resolution, the effect grants them haste until end of turn. Because this haste-granting effect starts applying only when the tokens enter the battlefield — which is after Dress Down was already on the battlefield — it falls under the same logic as [Dress Down ruling #0]: "If an effect grants a creature an ability after Dress Down has entered the battlefield, it won't lose that ability." Just as a land that becomes a creature after Dress Down is out keeps the abilities granted by whatever animated it, these Spirit tokens keep the haste granted to them at the moment of their creation, since that granting effect's timestamp is later than Dress Down's ability-stripping effect. The tokens have no other printed abilities to lose anyway (they're vanilla 1/1 Spirits aside from the haste grant).

Dress Down itself will still be sacrificed at the beginning of the end step per its own triggered ability [Dress Down text], since Dress Down isn't a creature here and hasn't lost that ability (see [Dress Down ruling #1] for what happens only if Dress Down itself becomes a creature, which isn't the case in this scenario).

This assumes Nehemiah cast Dress Down while Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's ability was still on the stack and unresolved, i.e., truly "in response." If instead Dress Down had already been on the battlefield well before Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance was even activated, the outcome is the same — the key fact is just that Dress Down entered before the tokens did.

question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?
answer:
Immediately after both effects resolve, Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 artifact land creature — specifically a Land Artifact Creature with the subtypes Mountain and Phyrexian Blinkmoth — that has flying and infect and can tap for {R}, but it no longer has its own printed mana ability or its own {1} activated ability. Next turn (once the 'until end of turn' effect from its own ability expires), it goes back to being just a Land — Mountain that can only tap for {R}; it has permanently lost its original {T}: Add {C} ability and its {1}: become-a-creature ability for as long as Blood Moon remains on the battlefield.

Here's why. Nikolas's activation of Inkmoth Nexus's own ability ('{1}: This land becomes a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn. It's still a land.') is put on the stack in response to Blood Moon, so it resolves first, before Blood Moon does. That ability is a type-changing effect (layer 4, applying the 'artifact creature' type and the 'Phyrexian Blinkmoth' creature subtype while Inkmoth Nexus keeps its land type per the 'still a land' clause, per [205.1b]), an ability-adding effect (layer 6, granting flying and infect), and a power/toughness-setting effect (layer 7b, setting it to 1/1) — all per [613.6] and [613.1d].

Blood Moon then resolves and applies its own layer-4 effect ('Nonbasic lands are Mountains') with a later timestamp than Inkmoth Nexus's own ability, since within a layer effects are applied in timestamp order unless dependency intervenes ([613.7], [613.3]). Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type is governed by [305.7]: Inkmoth Nexus loses its old land type (it had none) and, crucially, 'loses all abilities generated from its rules text' — that's its printed '{T}: Add {C}' ability and its '{1}: This land becomes...' ability — while gaining the appropriate basic-land mana ability, '{T}: Add {R}.' This matches Blood Moon's own rulings: nonbasic lands 'lose any other land types and abilities they had' and 'gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability "{T}: Add {R}"' [Blood Moon ruling #2]. Importantly, [305.7] also says this doesn't remove abilities 'granted to the land by other effects' — the flying, infect, artifact/creature typing, and 1/1 stats were granted by the separate, already-resolved effect of Inkmoth Nexus's own ability (not by the land's currently-printed rules text), so those survive Blood Moon's resolution and last until end of turn as originally set. Setting the land subtype also doesn't add or remove card types [305.7], so the artifact and creature types persist independently of the Mountain subtype. Blood Moon also doesn't grant the basic supertype or a new name [Blood Moon ruling #1], so Inkmoth Nexus remains a nonbasic land that is still affected by Blood Moon going forward.

At the start of the next turn, the 'until end of turn' duration on Inkmoth Nexus's own ability expires, so it stops being an artifact creature, loses the Phyrexian Blinkmoth subtype, its set 1/1 power/toughness, and flying/infect. question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
answer:
Urza's Saga is immediately sacrificed. Here's why: Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-setting effect (it sets a land's subtype to the basic land type Mountain). Under rule [305.7], when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, that land loses its old land type (here, the "Urza's Saga" land type) and "loses all abilities generated from its rules text" — this includes the abilities Urza's Saga has already gained from resolving Chapter I ("{T}: Add {C}") and Chapter II ("{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 ... Construct..."), as confirmed by [Urza's Saga ruling #5], since those abilities came from Urza's Saga's own rules text. It also loses its remaining chapter abilities (including the Chapter III search trigger and the lore-counter-adding trigger). In their place it gains the intrinsic mana ability of its new basic land type, "{T}: Add {R}" ([305.6], [Mountain]).

Crucially, this type-changing effect does not remove Urza's Saga's card types or supertypes ([305.7], [205.4b]): it is still an Enchantment Land with the Saga supertype, just as [Magus of the Moon ruling #1] notes that Magus of the Moon doesn't affect supertypes or names — Urza's Saga remains legendary/Saga and is not renamed "Mountain," it just now has the Mountain land subtype instead of the Urza's Saga subtype.

Because Urza's Saga is still a Saga permanent but has now lost all of its chapter abilities, [Urza's Saga ruling #1] and [Urza's Saga ruling #4] directly apply: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed." Magus of the Moon works exactly like that Blood Moon scenario, so the same result occurs here — the Saga sacrifice rule fires and Urza's Saga is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based/rule-mandated action once it has no chapter abilities left.

Note also [Magus of the Moon ruling #0]: even if Magus of the Moon itself later loses its abilities, the type-changing effect on nonbasic lands (including Urza's Saga) is applied in an earlier layer and continues to apply regardless, so this doesn't change the outcome here.

This analysis assumes the two-player or multiplayer distinction doesn't matter for this interaction — nothing about targeting a defending player or turn order is involved, so the result is the same regardless of how many players are in the game.

question: Nico controls [Dress Down], and Aya activates [Inkmoth Nexus]. What does it look like?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus becomes a 1/1 colorless Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact land creature that has flying and infect — it does NOT lose those two abilities to Dress Down, even though Dress Down's static ability says "Creatures lose all abilities." However, it does lose its own printed mana ability ("{T}: Add {C}") and its own activated ability ("{1}: This land becomes...") while it's a creature, because those get stripped along with everything else.

Here's why. Both effects modify abilities, which is layer 6 of the continuous-effects layer system [613.6] (rule 613.6 explicitly identifies ability-adding effects like "gains haste" as layer 6 effects, and the same layer governs ability-removing effects like Dress Down's). Two things are happening in layer 6 for Inkmoth Nexus: (1) Dress Down's continuous "Creatures lose all abilities" effect, and (2) the effect generated by Inkmoth Nexus's own activated ability, which grants it flying and infect (and makes it a creature via layer 4, per [613.6]'s type-changing discussion and [205.1b]'s "still a land" retention rule). Effects within the same layer are applied in the order they started to apply (their timestamp order), and rule [613.6] confirms that once an effect "starts to apply" in a layer it keeps being applied to that object.

In the scenario as given, Nico's Dress Down is already on the battlefield before Aya activates Inkmoth Nexus, so Dress Down's ability-stripping effect has the earlier timestamp. That means, in layer 6, Dress Down's "loses all abilities" is applied first — stripping Inkmoth Nexus's printed mana ability and its own activation ability — and only afterward does Inkmoth Nexus's own (newer) effect apply, adding flying and infect on top. The net result: a 1/1 artifact creature that's still a land, with flying and infect, but with no mana ability and no way to activate itself again for the rest of the turn.

Timing assumption: this all depends on Dress Down having entered the battlefield before Aya's activation of Inkmoth Nexus resolved, which is what the question states. If instead Inkmoth Nexus's ability had already resolved and given it flying/infect before Dress Down entered the battlefield, the timestamp order would flip and Dress Down (now the newer effect) would strip flying and infect along with everything else, leaving a vanilla 1/1 artifact land creature with no abilities at all.

question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
answer:
Painter's Servant becomes colorless (its natural color, since it has no colored mana symbols in its cost), and Dress Down stays blue. 

Here's why: Painter's Servant's printed ability reads "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors." Because Painter's Servant is itself a permanent, this ability also makes Painter's Servant itself blue — and since Painter's Servant's mana cost {2} has no colored symbols, it is normally colorless [202.2b], and per Painter's Servant ruling #0 a colorless object affected by this ability simply becomes the new color rather than being both colorless and blue.

However, Dress Down's text says "Creatures lose all abilities." Painter's Servant is an Artifact Creature — Scarecrow, so it is a creature and loses all of its abilities while Dress Down is on the battlefield, including the very static ability that grants blue to permanents (including itself). With that ability gone, there is no longer any effect making Painter's Servant blue [105.3, which allows effects to make a colored object become colorless, and 105.2c, which says a colorless object simply has no color]. So Painter's Servant reverts to being colorless.

Dress Down itself is unaffected by its own "creatures lose all abilities" clause because Dress Down is an enchantment, not a creature. Its color comes directly from its mana cost {1}{U}, which contains a blue mana symbol, so Dress Down is blue under rule 202.2b regardless of what's happening with Painter's Servant. (It would have been blue anyway even if Painter's Servant's ability were still functioning, since that ability only adds a color "in addition," per Painter's Servant ruling #5, and Dress Down was already blue.)

Note: this assumes Dress Down's static ability and Painter's Servant's static ability are both continuously checked as of the current game state (the normal way continuous effects work) — there's no timing ambiguity here since both are static, not one-shot, effects, so the order they were cast in doesn't matter; what matters is that Dress Down's "creatures lose all abilities" effect currently strips Painter's Servant of the ability that would otherwise color it blue.

question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?
answer:
Sunlit Marsh can still tap for one mana of any color. Blood Moon turns Sunlit Marsh (a nonbasic land, since it lacks the basic supertype even though it has the Plains and Swamp land types) into a Mountain: it loses its old land types (Plains Swamp) and the mana ability generated by its own rules text ("{T}: Add {W} or {B}"), and it gains the land type Mountain along with the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" (per rule 305.7 and Blood Moon ruling #2, plus the Mountain rule 305.6). However, rule 305.7 explicitly says this process 'doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects.' Urban Utopia's granted ability — 'Enchanted land has "{T}: Add one mana of any color"' — is exactly such an externally granted ability (Urban Utopia ruling #0 confirms the enchanted land keeps its other abilities), so Blood Moon does not strip it away. The net result is that Sunlit Marsh ends up with two mana abilities: the Mountain-based "{T}: Add {R}" and the Urban Utopia-based "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Since the second ability already lets you choose any single color (including red), Sunlit Marsh can be tapped to produce one mana of any color you choose.

question: Avery enchants their [Hall] with [Unbridled Growth]. Next turn, Nickolas casts [Blood Moon]. What colors of mana can Hall tap for?
answer:
Hall can still be tapped for one mana of any color, thanks to Unbridled Growth, and it can also add {R} as a Mountain — but it can no longer tap for {W} or use its investigate ability.

Here's why: Blood Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" sets Hall's land subtype. Hall is a nonbasic land (it's a named land, not one with a basic land type), so Blood Moon applies to it. Per rule [305.7], when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses all abilities generated from its own rules text (Hall's printed "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and its investigate ability go away), loses its old land type, and gains the mana ability for the new basic type — here, "{T}: Add {R}" for Mountain, per [305.6] and the Blood Moon ruling. Crucially, rule [305.7] explicitly says this "doesn't remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects." Unbridled Growth's text, "Enchanted land has '{T}: Add one mana of any color,'" grants Hall an ability from an outside source (the Aura), not from Hall's own rules text, so that granted ability survives Blood Moon's effect (this matches how granted abilities are treated as distinct from an object's own characteristics/text under [113.12]).

So after Blood Moon resolves, Hall is a Mountain with two mana abilities: the Mountain-derived "{T}: Add {R}" and the Unbridled Growth-granted "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Functionally, Hall can be tapped for any single color of mana you choose (white, blue, black, red, or green) when you use the ability from Unbridled Growth, or specifically red via its innate Mountain ability. It can no longer tap for {W} through its own printed ability, since that text is gone, and it no longer has the {4}, {T}: Investigate ability. This is a two-player-neutral interaction — nothing here depends on player count.
